1.1.title: The diamond and the field
1.1.objective: Recognize the whole field: the infield, the outfield and the foul lines.
demo: Welcome to the diamond! That's another name for a baseball field.
Look: the dirt part with the four corners is the infield.
The big green part in the back is the outfield.
And these two white lines going out to the sides are the foul lines: they separate fair territory from foul territory.

1.q: Tap the dirt part where the bases are
1.ok: That's it! That's where the bases are.
1.ko: Almost: look for the dirt part in the middle.

2.q: What's the big green part behind the infield called?
2.ko: Look again: it's the green part farthest from home plate.

3.q: The white lines on the sides are called foul lines
3.ko: It's true: that's what those lines are called.

4.q: Tap a foul line
4.ok: Nice tap!
4.ko: Not that one: the foul lines go out from home plate to the sides.

5.q: Why is the field called a diamond?
5.ko: Look at the shape of the infield: it looks like a diamond.

opts.shape: Because of its shape: it looks like a diamond
opts.money: Because it's worth a lot of money

6.q: Where do you play defense when the ball goes really far?
6.ok: Correct! Far away, in the outfield.
6.ko: Far from home plate: in the outfield.

1.2.title: The bases in order
1.2.objective: Run to first, second and third in the right order, always in the same direction.
demo: When you hit the ball, you don't run just anywhere: you run in order.
First, first base.
Then, second base.
Then, third base.
Always going around the same way, like a square. Watch me run it!

1.q: You hit the ball. Tap the first base you run to
1.ok: That's it! Always to first base first.
1.ko: No: your first stop is always first base.

2.q: After first base, which base is next?
2.ko: The order is 1, 2, 3: second base comes next.

3.q: Drag the runner around the bases in order, all the way to third
3.ko: You can't skip the order: first, second, then third.

4.q: A runner can run from first straight to third, skipping second
4.ok: Good! You have to touch every base.
4.ko: False: the runner has to touch second base on the way.

5.q: What shape does the path around the bases make?
5.ok: That's it! That's why it's called a diamond.
5.ko: Four corners: it's a square turned on its corner.

6.q: Tap third base
6.ok: Good! That's the last one before home plate.
6.ko: Third base is on the other side, right before home plate.

1.3.title: Home plate: where it all starts and ends
1.3.objective: Understand that you bat at home plate, you start running from home plate, and you score a run by touching home plate.
demo: This special corner isn't a base like the others: it's home plate.
This is where you stand to bat. This is where you start running.
And if you make it all the way around and touch home plate again, you scored a run!

1.q: Tap home plate
1.ok: That's it! The corner shaped like a little house.
1.ko: Home plate is the bottom corner, where you bat.

2.q: What do you do standing at home plate when your turn starts?
2.ok: Correct! That's where your turn starts.
2.ko: At home plate, it's your turn to bat.

3.q: When do you score a run?
3.ko: It only counts when you go all the way around and touch home plate.

opts.lap: When you touch home plate after going all the way around
opts.second: When you get to second base

4.q: Home plate is a square cushion like the other bases
4.ok: Good! Home plate is flat and pointed, like a little house.
4.ko: False: home plate is different, it's a flat plate.

5.q: The runner touched home plate. What was scored?
5.ok: Run! That's how you get a point in baseball.
5.ko: Touching home plate scores a run, not an out.

6.q: What are points called in baseball?
6.ko: There are no goals in baseball: there are runs.

1.4.title: The dugout and waiting your turn
1.4.objective: Know where the batting team waits, and that one player gets ready to bat next.
demo: And where does your team wait while it's batting? In the dugout: the long bench next to the field.
That's where players sit while they wait for their turn, with their helmet ready.
And the player who's up after the batter gets ready near home plate, in the on-deck circle.

1.q: Tap the dugout
1.ok: That's it! That's where the team waits.
1.ko: The dugout is the bench next to the field.

2.q: Who is in the dugout?
2.ok: Correct! The defense is out on the field.
2.ko: The team at bat waits in the dugout.

3.q: In the dugout you can take off your helmet and relax without paying attention to the game
3.ok: Good! Always pay attention: a foul ball can fly in.
3.ko: False: in the dugout you still pay attention to the game.

4.q: Who gets ready in the on-deck circle?
4.ok: That's it! On deck.
4.ko: The next batter gets ready there, helmet on.

5.q: What should you have ready in the dugout before your turn?
5.ok: Correct! Ready to go without making anyone wait.
5.ko: Your turn comes fast: helmet and bat ready.

6.q: A team's turn at bat ends. What happens to that team?
6.ok: That's it! The teams take turns.
6.ko: When a team finishes batting, it goes out to play defense.

opts.defend: It goes out to play defense

1.5.title: My baseball gear
1.5.objective: Tell apart the bat, glove, helmet and ball, and the golden rule: helmet on to bat and run the bases.
demo: To play, you need your gear.
The bat is for hitting the ball.
The glove is for catching it without it hurting.
The ball.
And the most important thing to keep you safe: the helmet. No helmet, no batting and no running the bases. Safety first!

1.q: What do you hit the ball with?
1.ko: You hit the ball with the bat.

2.q: What do you catch the ball with?
2.ko: You catch with the glove, on the hand you don't throw with.

3.q: The helmet protects your head when you bat and run the bases
3.ok: Yes! That's why you never take it off halfway.
3.ko: True: the helmet is protection, not decoration.

4.q: You're about to bat and you don't have a helmet. What do you do?
4.ok: Great! No helmet, no batting.
4.ko: Never bat without a helmet: ask for one first.

opts.ask: Ask for a helmet before batting
opts.cap: Bat with your cap on backwards

5.q: Tap the ball in the picture of the gear
5.ko: The round one with stitches is the ball.

6.q: Which hand does the glove go on if you throw with your right?
6.ok: Correct! You throw with one and catch with the other.
6.ko: The glove goes on the hand you don't throw with.

2.1.title: Pitcher and catcher: the battery
2.1.objective: Know that the pitcher throws from the mound and the catcher catches behind home plate, and that together they are called the battery.
demo: Every play starts with two players: the pitcher, who throws the ball from the mound, that little hill in the middle of the field.
And the catcher, who crouches behind home plate and catches it.
Together, the two of them are called the battery, because they are the engine of the team.

1.q: Tap where the pitcher stands
1.ok: That's it! The little hill in the middle.
1.ko: The pitcher throws from the mound, in the middle.

2.q: Where does the catcher go?
2.ko: The catcher goes behind home plate, ready to catch.

3.q: Who starts every play by throwing the ball?
3.ko: Everything starts with the pitcher's throw.

4.q: The pitcher and the catcher together are called the battery
4.ok: Yes! The battery.
4.ko: True: pitcher plus catcher make the battery.

5.q: What extra gear does the catcher wear for protection?
5.ok: Correct! The catcher gets fast balls, so they need protection.
5.ko: The catcher is fully protected: mask, chest protector and shin guards.

opts.gear: Mask, chest protector and shin guards

6.q: The catcher caught a pitch that went through the strike zone. What did the umpire call?
6.ok: Strike! You'll learn all about it in Level 4.
6.ko: If it went through the strike zone, the umpire calls a strike.

2.2.title: First and third: the corners
2.2.objective: Find the first baseman and the third baseman, and understand that they guard the two corners of the infield.
demo: There are two guards at the corners of the infield.
The first baseman guards first base: almost every play ends with a throw to him.
And the third baseman guards third base, close to where the hardest hits come on that side.
That's why third base is called the hot corner.

1.q: Tap the first baseman's position
1.ok: That's it! Right next to first base.
1.ko: The first baseman stands next to first base.

2.q: Tap the third baseman's position
2.ko: The third baseman guards the third-base corner.

3.q: Why does the first baseman catch so many throws?
3.ok: Correct! That's why he practices catching throws from everywhere.
3.ko: The most common out is at first base: that's why he gets so many.

opts.out: Because almost every play tries to get the out at first

4.q: Why is third base called the hot corner?
4.ok: That's it! The hot corner.
4.ko: The balls come so fast you have to react like lightning.

opts.hard: Because the hits come very hard and very fast
opts.dugout: Because it's close to the dugout

5.q: The first baseman can keep one foot on the base and stretch to catch the throw
5.ok: Yes! That way he gains a moment for the out.
5.ko: True: foot on the base and stretch for the ball.

6.q: Drag each player to his corner
6.ko: Each one to his corner: check which is first and which is third.
6.answer: First baseman at first, third baseman at third

2.3.title: Second and shortstop: the middle
2.3.objective: Find the second baseman and the shortstop, and understand that they cover the middle of the infield and second base.
demo: Two teammates play in the middle of the infield: the second baseman and the shortstop.
Together they guard the middle and take turns covering second base when there is a throw or a runner.
They're like a team inside the team.

1.q: Tap where the shortstop plays
1.ko: The shortstop plays between second and third.

2.q: Tap where the second baseman plays
2.ko: The second baseman plays between first and second.

3.q: Why does second base need two players to cover it?
3.ok: Correct! The second baseman and the shortstop take turns.
3.ko: Nobody stands on second all the time: they cover it in turns.

opts.nobody: Because nobody plays standing on it all the time

4.q: The shortstop plays between second and third base
4.ok: Yes! That's the shortstop's spot.
4.ko: True: the shortstop covers the space between second and third.

5.q: A ground ball goes right up the middle. Who can get to that ball?
5.ok: That's it! The middle is their zone.
5.ko: Those two guard the middle of the infield.

opts.middle: The second baseman or the shortstop

6.q: Drag the shortstop and the second baseman to their correct side
6.ko: Remember: shortstop near third, second baseman near first.
6.answer: Shortstop on the left of the infield, second baseman on the right

2.4.title: The three outfielders
2.4.objective: Find the left, center and right fielders, and understand that the center fielder covers the most ground and backs up the other two.
demo: Behind the infield, in the outfield, three players play: the left fielder, the center fielder and the right fielder.
They catch the high, long hits and throw the ball back to the infield fast.
The one in the middle covers the most space and is the leader of the three.
Left and right are named looking from home plate out to the field.

1.q: Tap where the center fielder plays
1.ko: The center fielder plays in the middle of the outfield.

2.q: How many outfielders are there?
2.ko: There are three outfielders, one for each zone.

3.q: Outfielders are named looking from home plate out to the field
3.ok: Yes! That's why the left fielder is on that side when you look from home plate.
3.ko: True: you look from home plate, not from the outfield.

4.q: Which outfielder covers the most ground?
4.ok: That's it! He runs to both sides.
4.ko: The center fielder covers the biggest space.

5.q: The ball went over the infield, very far. Who goes after it?
5.ko: Far away is outfielder territory: they go get it.

6.q: Drag each outfielder to his zone
6.ko: Look from home plate: left, center, right.
6.answer: Left, center and right, in order from home plate

2.5.title: The 9 positions and their numbers
2.5.objective: Memorize the official number of each position: 1 pitcher, 2 catcher, 3 first, 4 second, 5 third, 6 shortstop, 7 left, 8 center, 9 right.
demo: Last secret of this level: every position has a number, and it is the same all over the world.
One, pitcher.
Two, catcher.
Three, first baseman.
Four, second baseman.
Five, third baseman.
Six, shortstop.
Seven, left fielder.
Eight, center fielder.
Nine, right fielder.
That's how scorekeepers write down the games.

1.q: What is the pitcher's number?
1.ok: That's it! The pitcher is always number 1.
1.ko: The pitcher starts the count: number 1.

2.q: What is the catcher's number?
2.ko: After the pitcher comes the catcher: number 2.

3.q: Tap position number 6
3.ko: Number 6 is the shortstop, between second and third.

4.q: Which position is number 8?
4.ok: That's it! Center fielder, number 8.
4.ko: Number 8 is the center fielder.

5.q: Position numbers change in every league
5.ko: False: 1 to 9 is the same in all of baseball.

6.q: Put the cards in order from 1 to 4: pitcher, catcher, first, second
6.ko: In order: pitcher 1, catcher 2, first 3, second 4.

3.1.title: The inning: top and bottom
3.1.objective: Understand that an inning has two halves: in the top the visiting team bats, and in the bottom the home team bats.
demo: A game is split into little pieces called innings.
Every inning has two halves.
In the top of the inning, the visiting team bats.
When they get three outs, the bottom of the inning comes, and the home team bats.
Top and bottom: that is one whole inning.

1.q: What is each big piece of the game called?
1.ko: Those pieces are called innings.

2.q: How many halves does an inning have?
2.ko: An inning is two turns, one for each team.

3.q: Who bats in the top of the inning?
3.ok: That's it! The visitors go first.
3.ko: In the top, the visiting team bats.

4.q: Who bats in the bottom of the inning?
4.ok: Correct! That's why they sometimes decide the game at the end.
4.ko: In the bottom, it's the home team's turn.

5.q: If only the top half has been played, the inning is over
5.ok: Good! The bottom half is still missing.
5.ko: False: the inning ends when both teams have batted.

6.q: The top of the third inning is over. What comes next?
6.ok: That's it! Now the home team bats.
6.ko: Next is the bottom of that same inning.

3.2.title: Three outs and switch
3.2.objective: Know that a team's turn at bat ends when the defense gets three outs, and then the teams switch places.
demo: How long does a turn at bat last? Until you get three outs.
One,
two,
three outs, and switch:
the team that was batting goes out to play defense, and the team that was on defense comes in to bat.
That's why in baseball nobody keeps batting the whole game.

1.q: How many outs end a team's turn?
1.ko: It takes three outs per turn.

2.q: There are already 2 outs and they make the third. What happens?
2.ko: Third out: the turn is over.

3.q: The outs from one half don't add to the other half: every turn starts at zero
3.ok: Yes! Every turn is a new count.
3.ko: True: each team counts its own three outs in its turn.

4.q: Your team was on the field playing defense and you got the 3 outs. Where do you go?
4.ok: That's it! Now it's your turn to bat.
4.ko: Defense is over: your turn at bat begins.

opts.dugout: To the dugout, to get ready to bat
opts.outfield: To the outfield to keep waiting

5.q: A team has 0 outs. How long does it keep batting?
5.ok: Correct! With no outs, the turn is still alive.
5.ko: The turn has no clock: it ends with the third out.

opts.untilThree: It keeps batting until it gets 3 outs

6.q: Third out in the top of the inning. What does the game announce now?
6.ko: Third out in the top: switch, here comes the bottom.

opts.change: Switch: here comes the bottom of the inning

3.3.title: How to score a run
3.3.objective: Explain that a run only counts when the runner goes around all the bases in order and touches home plate without being put out.
demo: You already know how to get to home plate.
Now the whole rule: to score a run you start as the batter, touch first, second and third in order, and touch home plate without being put out along the way.
If you're put out before you get there, there is no run.
Every time a runner makes it all the way home, that's one run.

1.q: What does a runner need to score?
1.ko: Without the whole trip, there is no run.

opts.all: Touch all the bases in order and reach home plate

2.q: If the runner is put out between third and home, the run still counts
2.ok: Good! Out before home plate means no run.
2.ko: False: the runner has to touch home plate without being out.

3.q: Drag the runner along the path to score
3.ko: The trip is complete: the three bases and back to home plate.
3.answer: Start at home and come back to home through all three bases

4.q: A runner is on third base. What is left to score?
4.ok: Correct! One more step.
4.ko: From third, all that is left is touching home plate.

5.q: Who can score during a turn at bat?
5.ok: That's it! Every runner who completes the trip adds a run.
5.ko: Every runner who touches home plate scores a run.

opts.runners: The runners who reach home plate
opts.batter: Only the one who is batting

6.q: The score is 4 to 2. Your team scores another run. What is the score now?
6.ko: 4 plus 1 run: 5 to 2.

3.4.title: The batting order
3.4.objective: Understand that batters follow a list in order (the lineup), that nobody can be skipped, and that the order picks up where it left off in the next inning.
demo: Nobody bats whenever they want: there is a list called the lineup.
The first one bats, then the second, then the third, and so on.
If the turn ended with batter number four in one inning, number five starts the next inning.
The order is never skipped.

1.q: What is the list of batters in order called?
1.ko: That ordered list is the lineup.

2.q: A player can bat twice in a row if they are the best on the team
2.ok: Good! The order is always followed.
2.ko: False: the next one on the list bats, whoever it is.

3.q: The turn ended with batter 4. Who leads off the next inning?
3.ok: Correct! The order continues where it left off.
3.ko: You don't go back to 1: number 5 is next.

4.q: Number 7 just batted. The turn isn't over. Who is next?
4.ok: That's it! One after another.
4.ko: After 7 comes 8.

5.q: What happens when the list reaches the last batter and the turn keeps going?
5.ok: Correct! The wheel goes around again.
5.ko: The list is a wheel: after the last one comes the first.

6.q: A team sent up someone to bat whose turn it wasn't. What is wrong?
6.ok: That's it! The order is a rule, not a suggestion.
6.ko: Batting out of turn is against the rules.

3.5.title: Who wins the game
3.5.objective: Explain that the team with more runs when the innings are done wins, and that the number of innings depends on the league and the age group.
demo: So who wins? Easy: when the innings are over, the team with more runs wins.
Watch out for this: not every game lasts the same.
In many kids leagues they play 6 innings,
and in grown-up baseball, 9.
Your coach will tell you how many your league plays.
And if it's tied at the end, in many cases they play an extra inning to break the tie, depending on the league's rules.

1.q: Who wins the game?
1.ko: Not outs, not hits: runs win.

opts.moreRuns: The team with more runs at the end
opts.moreOuts: The team that makes more outs

2.q: Every baseball game lasts exactly 9 innings
2.ok: Good! Kids leagues usually play fewer, like 6.
2.ko: False: the length changes by league and by age.

3.q: End of the game: 6 runs to 4. Who won?
3.ko: The one with more wins: the team with 6.

4.q: It is tied when the planned innings are over. What can happen, depending on the league?
4.ok: That's it! An extra inning to break the tie.
4.ko: Many leagues break the tie with one more inning.

opts.allbat: Everyone bats again at the same time
opts.repeat: Always replay the game another day

5.q: Your kids league team is going to play. Who tells you for sure how many innings the game lasts?
5.ok: Correct! Every league has its own number.
5.ko: Ask your coach: it depends on your league.

opts.coach: Your coach, based on your league

6.q: The last out was made and one team is winning by 1 run. What comes next?
6.ko: Last out with a lead: the game is over.

opts.over: The game is over: that team won
opts.untilTie: They play until it is tied

4.1.title: Ball and strike
4.1.objective: Tell a strike (a good pitch, in the zone or swung at) from a ball (a pitch outside the zone that the batter doesn't swing at).
demo: Watch every pitch closely, because the umpire calls one of two things.
If the ball goes through the strike zone, or if you swing and miss, it's a strike.
If it goes far from the zone and you didn't swing, it's a ball.
A ball is bad for the pitcher and good for you.
The count of balls and strikes is the score of your turn at bat.

1.q: The pitch went through the middle of the zone and the batter didn't swing
1.ok: Called strike! Even without a swing, if it's in the zone it's a strike.
1.ko: It went through the strike zone: that's a strike.

2.q: The pitch was way too high and the batter didn't swing
2.ok: Ball! Way out of the zone.
2.ko: Way too high and no swing: it's a ball.

3.q: The batter swung and missed the ball
3.ok: Swinging strike! Swinging and missing is a strike too.
3.ko: If you swing and miss, it's a strike even if the pitch was bad.

4.q: If the pitch is outside the zone but the batter swings and misses, it's a ball
4.ok: Good! A swing and a miss is always a strike.
4.ko: False: a missed swing turns any pitch into a strike.

5.q: Who calls whether it was a ball or a strike?
5.ko: The umpire stands behind the catcher and makes the call.

6.q: The pitch goes straight into the dirt and the batter doesn't swing. What is it?
6.ko: Into the dirt and no swing: ball.

4.2.title: The strike zone
4.2.objective: Recognize the strike zone: the imaginary rectangle over home plate, between the batter's knees and chest in their normal stance.
demo: Imagine an invisible rectangle floating over home plate: that is the strike zone.
It is as wide as home plate,
and about as tall as from the batter's knees to their chest, standing normally.
If the ball crosses through that rectangle, it's a strike.
If it goes outside, it's a ball.
It's imaginary, but the umpire sees it.

1.q: Tap where the strike zone is
1.ok: That's it! It floats over home plate.
1.ko: The zone is over home plate, not over first base or the mound.
1.answer: Over home plate, in front of the batter

2.q: How wide is the strike zone?
2.ok: Correct! Exactly as wide as home plate.
2.ko: The zone is the same width as home plate.

opts.field: As wide as the whole field

3.q: The height of the zone goes roughly from
3.ok: That's it! In their normal batting stance.
3.ko: Knees to chest: that is about how tall it is.

opts.kneesChest: The batter's knees to their chest

4.q: The ball crossed inside the rectangle, at waist height
4.ok: Strike! It crossed the zone.
4.ko: Inside the rectangle is a strike.

5.q: The ball went past the outside of the rectangle and the batter didn't swing
5.ko: Outside the rectangle and no swing: ball.

6.q: The strike zone changes a little with how tall each batter is
6.ok: Yes! A tall kid has a higher zone than a short kid.
6.ko: True: it fits each batter's body.

4.3.title: The foul ball
4.3.objective: Understand that a ball hit outside the lines before it passes the bases is a foul: it counts as a strike, but with two strikes it doesn't end the turn, and if a fielder catches it in the air it's an out.
demo: When you hit the ball and it goes outside the foul lines, it's a foul ball.
A foul counts as a strike,
but listen to the trick: if you already have two strikes and you hit a foul, you don't strike out.
You keep batting.
And watch out: if a fielder catches that foul in the air, before it lands, it is an out.

1.q: What is a foul?
1.ko: A foul is a ball that goes outside the fair area.

opts.outside: A ball hit outside the foul lines

2.q: The batted ball landed outside the third-base line
2.ko: It landed in foul territory: foul.

3.q: A foul that lands on the ground counts as
3.ko: A foul on the ground is one more strike in the count.

4.q: With two strikes, a foul that lands on the ground is the third strike and you strike out
4.ok: Good! A foul doesn't strike you out: you keep batting.
4.ko: False, and it's the key trick: a foul with 2 strikes is not a strikeout.

5.q: The third baseman caught the foul in the air, before it landed. What happens?
5.ok: That's it! Caught in the air: out.
5.ko: A foul caught in the air is an out, wherever it is.

6.q: The count is 3 balls and 2 strikes, and the batter hits a foul that lands on the ground. What is the count now?
6.ok: Exactly! The famous full count stays alive.
6.ko: Foul with 2 strikes: the count doesn't change, it stays 3-2.

4.4.title: Strikeout and walk
4.4.objective: Know that three strikes end the batter's turn with a strikeout, and four balls send them walking to first base (a walk, or base on balls).
demo: The count has two endings without hitting the ball.
If you get three strikes, you struck out: that's a strikeout, and you're out.
But if the pitcher throws four balls first, you win the turn: you walk to first base and they can't put you out.
That's called a walk, or base on balls.
The count is always said with balls first and then strikes: 3 and 2 means three balls and two strikes.

1.q: How many strikes does it take to strike out?
1.ko: Three strikes: strikeout, and out.

2.q: How many balls does it take for the batter to walk to first?
2.ok: Correct! A walk: time to walk.
2.ko: Four balls: a walk.

3.q: The count is 3 balls and 0 strikes. Another pitch comes outside the zone. What happens?
3.ok: That's it! Ball four: walk to first.
3.ko: That was ball four: a walk.

4.q: The count is 0 balls and 2 strikes. A called strike comes in. What happens?
4.ok: Strikeout! Strike three.
4.ko: That was strike three: out on a strikeout.

opts.k: Struck out, it is an out

5.q: The count is said with strikes first and then balls
5.ok: Good! Balls come first: 3 and 2 means 3 balls and 2 strikes.
5.ko: False: balls first, strikes second.

6.q: Ball four in this turn, way outside. What does the batter get to do?
6.ok: Walk! Off to first, nice and easy.
6.ko: Four balls: the batter goes to first without being out.

opts.dugout: Go back to the dugout as an out

4.5.title: Hit by pitch and full count
4.5.objective: Understand that if a pitch hits the batter when they didn't try to get hit and didn't swing, they go to first base (hit by pitch), and review the full count, 3-2.
demo: Last lesson about the count.
If the pitch hits the batter (and they didn't swing or step into it on purpose), it's not an out and they don't keep batting: they go to first base.
That's called a hit by pitch.
Now put it all together: the most exciting count is 3 balls and 2 strikes, the full count.
The next pitch almost always decides it: a ball and you walk, a strike and you strike out.

1.q: The pitch hit the batter on the leg and they didn't swing. What happens?
1.ko: Hit without a swing: to first base.

opts.strike: It's a strike and they keep batting

2.q: If the batter swings, it doesn't count as hit by pitch even if the ball hits them
2.ok: Good! With a swing, it's a strike.
2.ko: True: the swing turns the play into a strike.

3.q: What is the count of 3 balls and 2 strikes called?
3.ko: 3 and 2: a full count, everything is on the line.

4.q: Full count and a pitch comes in outside
4.ok: Walk! Ball four on a full count.
4.ko: That was ball four: to first.

5.q: Full count, the batter swings and misses
5.ko: Swung and missed strike three: strikeout.

6.q: Full count and the batter hits a foul that lands on the ground
6.ok: Perfect! A foul with 2 strikes doesn't decide anything.
6.ko: Just like in Lesson 4.3: the foul keeps the turn alive.

opts.keep: Still a full count: bat again

5.1.title: The hit
5.1.objective: Understand what a hit is: a good batted ball that gets the batter safely to a base without the defense making a mistake.
demo: It's time to really hit!
When you hit the ball and get safely to a base, without the defense making a mistake, that's a hit.
The ball can roll on the ground between the fielders, or land in the outfield where nobody catches it.
If you get there safely, your hit counts!
And remember: while you're standing on your base, you're safe. Nobody can get you out.

1.q: What is a hit?
1.ko: A hit is when you hit the ball and reach base safely.

opts.a: A batted ball that gets you on base safely
opts.b: A batted ball that is caught in the air

2.q: For it to be a hit, the ball has to leave the field
2.ok: Good! A hit can be a short one.
2.ko: False: you just need to reach base safely.

3.q: Which picture shows a hit?
3.ok: Correct! It landed where nobody caught it.
3.ko: If it's caught in the air, it's an out, not a hit.

opts.a: The ball lands in the outfield and the batter reaches first
opts.b: The ball is caught in the air

4.q: You reached first before the throw. What does the umpire call?
4.ok: Safe! You got there safely.
4.ko: Safe means you made it: you got there first.

opts.a: Safe!

5.q: You hit a short one. Tap the base you reach first
5.ok: Good! First base is your first stop.
5.ko: Every hit starts by reaching first.

6.q: You reach the base before the ball. What's the word for that?
6.ko: When you make it before the ball, you're safe.

opts.a: Safe

5.2.title: Single, double and triple
5.2.objective: Name each hit by the bases it is worth: a single is one, a double two and a triple three, and stop at the right base by watching the ball and the coach.
demo: A hit is named by the bases you reach.
If you reach first: it's a single.
If the ball goes far and you reach second: it's a double.
And if you run and run and reach third: a triple!
The triple is the hardest: you have to hit it far and run like the wind.
Keep going or stop? Watch the ball and listen to your coach: they can see the whole field.

1.q: You reached first with your hit. What did you hit?
1.ko: One base: a single.

opts.a: A single

2.q: The ball went far into the outfield and you reached second. What is it?
2.ko: Two bases: a double.

opts.a: A double

3.q: You hit it really far and ran all the way to third. What is it?
3.ko: Three bases: a triple.

opts.a: A triple

4.q: Drag each hit to its base: single, double, triple
4.ok: Perfect! One, two and three.
4.ko: Count the bases: 1 single, 2 double, 3 triple.
4.answer: Single to first, double to second, triple to third

5.q: The triple is the easiest hit to get
5.ko: False: a triple takes a long hit and a lot of running.

6.q: You're running to second and don't know whether to keep going. Who do you look at?
6.ko: Watch the ball and listen to the coach.

opts.a: The coach and the ball

5.3.title: The home run and the ground rule double
5.3.objective: Understand the home run (the ball leaves the field in the air over fair territory: a full trip around) and the ground rule double: if a fair ball bounces and then leaves the field, everyone gets two bases, not a home run.
demo: The most famous hit: the home run.
The ball flies out of the field, in fair territory, without touching the ground: you go all the way around and score.
But watch out for its cousin: if the ball bounces in fair territory and THEN goes over the fence, it is not a home run.
It's a ground rule double: the batter goes to second and every runner moves up two bases.
Did it go out in the air? Home run. Did it bounce first? Ground rule double.

1.q: The ball leaves the field in the air, in fair territory. What is it?
1.ok: Home run! All the way around.
1.ko: In the air and out: a home run.

opts.a: A home run

2.q: The ball bounces in the outfield and goes over the fence. What is it?
2.ok: That's it! It bounced first: two bases.
2.ko: If it bounces and goes out, it's a ground rule double, not a home run.

opts.a: A ground rule double

3.q: On a ground rule double, the batter scores a run
3.ok: Good! They go to second, they don't score.
3.ko: False: on a ground rule double they reach second.

4.q: The ball bounced and left the field. How many bases does the umpire give?
4.ok: Two bases! Ground rule double.
4.ko: It bounced and went out: two bases for everyone.

opts.a: Two bases

5.q: On a home run, how many bases do you run?
5.ok: Correct! And you score a run.
5.ko: A home run goes around the whole diamond.

opts.a: All of them: all the way around to home

6.q: Drag each hit to its result: out in the air / bounces and goes out
6.ko: Remember: the bounce changes everything.
6.answer: In the air: home run; bounces and goes out: ground rule double

5.4.title: Running to first
5.4.objective: Learn that when running to first you can overrun the base without having to come right back, but at second and third, overrunning puts you in danger of an out.
demo: You ran to first and got there safe. Nice!
First base has a special rule: you can run past it, keep running a little into foul territory, and come back calmly without being tagged out, as long as you don't try to go to second.
But careful: second and third don't have that rule.
If you run past the base, they can tag you with the ball and you are out.
First base forgives; the others do not.

1.q: At which base can you run past and come back safely?
1.ko: Only first base lets you do that.

opts.a: At first

2.q: If you run past second, they can't get you out either
2.ok: Good! At second they can tag you.
2.ko: False: away from first, running past is dangerous.

3.q: You ran past first and turn as if to go to second. What happens?
3.ok: Correct! If you try to advance, the play is on.
3.ko: First forgives running past, not trying to advance.

opts.a: The defense can get you out

4.q: Tap the base you can run past when you get there
4.ok: Good! That's the one.
4.ko: Only first base lets you run past it.

5.q: Which runner is in danger?
5.ko: Second doesn't forgive running past.

opts.a: The one who ran past second
opts.b: The one who ran past first and is coming back
opts.c: The one standing on their base

6.q: You reached first, ran past a little and came straight back. What does the umpire call?
6.ko: You came straight back: safe.

opts.a: Safe!

5.5.title: The bunt
5.5.objective: Understand the bunt: holding the bat without swinging to let the ball drop softly, and that a foul bunt with two strikes is strike three.
demo: Not every hit is aiming for the fence.
A bunt means holding the bat firmly, without swinging, and letting the ball drop softly in front of home plate.
It can surprise the defense or move a teammate up.
And learn this one, because it is special: if you bunt foul with two strikes, that foul DOES count as strike three and you are out.
In Level 4 you learned that a foul with two strikes is not a strikeout; with a bunt, the story changes.

1.q: What is a bunt?
1.ko: Bunt: the bat stays still and the ball goes soft.

opts.a: Letting the ball drop softly by holding the bat, without swinging

2.q: On a bunt you take the hardest swing of the game
2.ko: False: you hold the bat, you don't swing it hard.

3.q: You bunt foul with two strikes. What happens?
3.ko: Foul bunt with two strikes: strikeout.

opts.a: It's strike three: out

4.q: Which picture shows a bunt?
4.ok: That's it! Bat firm and still.
4.ko: This is what a bunt looks like.

opts.a: The bat held across, with no swing
opts.b: The bat swinging all the way

5.q: The bunt went foul with two strikes. What does the umpire call?
5.ko: With a bunt there is no free foul on two strikes.

opts.a: Out! Strike three

6.q: What is a surprise bunt for?
6.ko: Defense far back: the bunt can be a hit.

opts.a: To reach first when the defense is far back

6.1.title: The caught fly ball
6.1.objective: Reinforce that any batted ball caught in the air, before it touches the ground, is an out for the batter: a fly ball, a line drive and even a fly ball in foul territory.
demo: Baseball's fastest rule: if the batted ball is caught in the air, before it bounces, the batter is out.
It doesn't matter if it's a high fly ball to the outfield or a hard line drive: a catch is a catch.
It even counts in foul territory, if the fielder catches it in the air.
But if it bounces first, nobody can 'catch' it for the out anymore: you have to play it off the ground.

1.q: The outfielder catches your fly ball in the air. What happens?
1.ok: Correct! Caught in the air: out.
1.ko: Ball caught in the air: batter out.

opts.a: You're out

2.q: A line drive caught in the air is also an out
2.ok: Yes! Line drive or fly ball, same thing.
2.ko: True: what matters is catching it in the air.

3.q: The ball bounces in the outfield and then the outfielder picks it up. Was it caught for an out?
3.ok: That's it! It bounced: no catch.
3.ko: For an out in the air, it can't bounce.

opts.a: No, it already bounced

4.q: Which batted ball is a sure out if caught?
4.ok: Correct! That one is caught in the air.
4.ko: You go for the fly ball in the air.

opts.a: A high fly ball to the outfield

5.q: The shortstop catches a screaming line drive. What does the umpire call for the batter?
5.ko: Caught in the air is always an out.

opts.a: Out!

6.q: A foul fly ball caught in the air is an out
6.ok: Good! In foul territory catching it counts too.
6.ko: True: a catch in foul territory counts.

6.2.title: The force out
6.2.objective: Understand the force out: if the runner has to move up, a fielder with the ball only needs to step on the base before the runner gets there.
demo: Imagine a line that pushes.
When the batter makes contact and has to go to first, everyone behind pushes: the runner on first has to go to second.
That runner is forced.
And here's the good news for the defense: they don't have to tag him.
They just step on his base with the ball before he gets there: a force out. Step on it and that's it.

1.q: What is a force out?
1.ko: Forced: you step on the base with the ball.

opts.a: Stepping on the base with the ball before the forced runner
opts.b: Tagging the runner with an empty glove

2.q: On a force out you have to tag the runner with the ball
2.ok: Good! Stepping on the base is enough.
2.ko: False: stepping on the base is enough.

3.q: Runner on first, ground ball to the shortstop. The shortstop steps on second with the ball before the runner. What happens?
3.ko: He was pushed from first: forced.

opts.a: Force out at second

4.q: Forced runner running to second. Tap the base the fielder must step on with the ball
4.ok: Good! Step on second and he's out.
4.ko: The forced runner's base is the target.

5.q: The fielder stepped on the base with the ball before the forced runner. What does the umpire call?
5.ko: The ball got to the base first: out.

opts.a: Out!

6.q: Why do we say the runner is "forced"?
6.ko: The batter-runner pushes him from behind.

opts.a: Because the one behind pushes him: he can't stay
opts.c: Because the coach makes him steal

6.3.title: Tagging the runner out
6.3.objective: Understand the tag out: when the runner isn't forced, you have to touch him with the ball, or with the glove holding the ball, while he is off his base.
demo: And if the runner does NOT have to run, stepping on the base doesn't work.
You have to touch him: a tag out.
You touch him with the ball, or with the glove if the ball is inside it, held tight.
And it only counts while the runner is off his base: on his base, he's safe.
If he's standing on it, tagging him does nothing.

1.q: What is a tag out?
1.ko: With no force, you have to tag the runner.

opts.a: Touching the runner with the ball while off his base

2.q: Tagging the runner with an empty glove, without the ball, is an out
2.ok: Good! The ball is what counts.
2.ko: False: without the ball there's no tag.

3.q: The runner is standing on his base and gets tagged with the ball. Is he out?
3.ok: Correct! On the base he's safe.
3.ko: On his base, he's safe.

opts.a: No, on his base he's safe

4.q: The runner stepped off second and is away from the base. Tap who has to be tagged with the ball
4.ok: Good! Him, with the ball.
4.ko: Off the base, you tag the runner.

5.q: Which tag counts for an out?
5.ok: That's it! Ball held tight and tag.
5.ko: The ball has to be secure in the glove.

opts.a: The glove holding the ball tight touches the runner
opts.b: An empty glove brushes the runner
opts.c: A hand with no ball touches the runner

6.q: They tagged the runner with the ball halfway between bases. What does the umpire call?
6.ko: Off his base and tagged: out.

opts.a: Out!

6.4.title: Forced or not?
6.4.objective: Decide, based on who is behind, whether a runner is forced (just step on the base) or not (you have to tag him). The key: whether the base behind is taken by someone pushing him.
demo: Before you play, ask yourself: is this runner forced or not?
The key is to look behind.
If someone behind him needs his base, he's forced and you just step on the base.
If nobody is coming behind, he's not forced: you have to tag him.
Example: a runner alone on second. Nobody pushes him (there's no runner on first), so to get him out you have to tag him with the ball.
Look behind and you'll know what to do.

1.q: Runner alone on second, ground ball to the infield. Is he forced to go to third?
1.ko: With nobody on first, there's no force at second.

opts.a: No, nobody pushes him

2.q: Runners on first and second, ground ball. Is the runner on second forced?
2.ok: That's it! The whole line pushes.
2.ko: With first taken, the runner on second is forced too.

opts.a: Yes, the runner on first and the batter push him

3.q: To decide if there is a force, you look at whether the base behind is taken
3.ko: True: look behind.

4.q: Runner alone on third. To get him out between bases you have to:
4.ok: Correct! He's never forced.
4.ko: The runner on third alone is never forced: you tag him.

opts.a: Tag him with the ball

5.q: Runners on first and second. Tap the runner who is forced to go to third
5.ko: The one on second, pushed by the runner on first.

6.q: Runner alone on second: the fielder steps on third with the ball but doesn't tag the runner, who goes back to second. What does the umpire call?
6.ok: Safe! He had to be tagged.
6.ko: Without a force, stepping on the base doesn't work.

opts.a: Safe! There was no force

6.5.title: The double play and the fielder's choice
6.5.objective: Understand the double play (two outs on one play, usually at second and first) and the fielder's choice: the defense chooses to go for another out and the batter reaches first without a hit.
demo: Two outs with a single batted ball? It's called a double play.
The recipe: runner on first, ground ball to the infield, throw to second for the first out and a throw to first for the second!
That's why it's scored 6-4-3 and things like that, as you'll see in Level 8.
And listen to this one: sometimes the defense chooses to throw to another base and the batter reaches first.
That's not a hit or an error: it's a fielder's choice.
The defense made a choice, and it worked or it didn't.

1.q: What is a double play?
1.ko: Two outs, one play.

opts.a: Two outs on the same play

2.q: Classic double play recipe: runner on first and a ground ball. The defense throws:
2.ko: The short way: 6-4-3.

opts.a: To second and then to first

3.q: The defense throws to second going for an out and the batter reaches first. He got there on:
3.ko: Fielder's choice: they chose another out.

opts.a: A fielder's choice

4.q: A double play on the ground almost always needs a forced runner
4.ok: Good! No force, no recipe.
4.ko: True: the double play comes from the force.

5.q: Throw to second: out. Throw to first: out. How many outs did the umpire call on the play?
5.ko: Two out calls on one play.

opts.a: Two outs

6.q: On a fielder's choice, the batter reaches first because:
6.ko: It's not a hit: the defense chose.

opts.a: The defense chose to go for another out

7.1.title: Safe on the base: your safe spot
7.1.objective: Understand that standing on the base the runner is safe, that only one runner can be on a base and what happens if two end up on the same one.
demo: Your base is your safe spot.
Standing on it, with the ball live, nobody can tag you out.
But it only has room for one: two runners can't share a base.
If the runner behind catches you on the same base, one of you is extra, and almost always the one who came from behind is in danger, because the runner ahead already owned that base.
One base, one runner.

1.q: Standing on your base, can they get you out by tagging you with the ball?
1.ko: On your base you're safe.

opts.a: No, it's my safe spot

2.q: Two runners can be on one base at the same time without a problem
2.ko: False: one base, one runner.

3.q: Two runners end up on second. Who is in danger?
3.ok: Correct! The first one owned it.
3.ko: That base already belonged to the runner ahead.

opts.a: The one who came from behind
opts.b: The one who was already there

4.q: Tap the safe spot of the runner on third
4.ok: Good! That's his safe spot.
4.ko: Standing there, he's safe.

5.q: You're standing on your base and they tag you with the ball. What does the umpire call?
5.ko: On your base there is no tag out.

opts.a: Safe!

6.q: You leave your base, get halfway, and they tag you with the ball. What happens?
6.ok: Correct! Off your base, you're in danger.
6.ko: Away from your base, the tag is an out.

opts.a: Out: you left your safe spot

7.2.title: Tag up
7.2.objective: Understand tagging up: on a caught fly ball, the runner has to be touching his base when it's caught and only then can run; if he leaves early, he can be called out on appeal.
demo: A fly ball goes up and you're on base.
Your first instinct is to run. No!
If they catch the ball and you've already left, the defense can throw the ball back to your base and you're out.
The right play is called tagging up: you stay touching your base, wait for the catch, and the instant the ball touches the glove, you go!
Touch, wait for the catch and run.

1.q: What is tagging up?
1.ko: First the catch, then you go.

opts.a: Waiting on your base for the catch and running after

2.q: You can leave your base as soon as the batter swings
2.ok: Good! You have to wait for the catch.
2.ko: False: leaving early puts you in danger.

3.q: You left before the catch and the ball was caught. The defense throws the ball back to your base. What happens?
3.ko: That's why you touch and wait.

opts.a: You're out

4.q: You're on third and a fly ball goes to the outfield. Tap where you have to be when it's caught
4.ok: Good! Touching third, ready to go.
4.ko: Your foot stays on the base until the catch.

5.q: They caught the fly ball, you took off right as the ball landed in the glove, and you reached home. What does the umpire call?
5.ko: You waited for the catch: a legal play.

opts.a: Safe! The run counts

6.q: At exactly what moment can you take off when tagging up?
6.ko: Ball in the glove: go!

opts.a: When the ball touches the fielder's glove

7.3.title: If the batted ball hits you
7.3.objective: Learn that if a fair batted ball touches a runner before passing a fielder, the runner is out and the ball is dead; and the exception: if the ball has already passed a fielder (other than the pitcher) and no other fielder can play it, the runner is not out and play goes on.
demo: You're running and the batted ball hits you.
It's almost always bad for you: if the fair ball touches you before passing a fielder, you're out and the ball is dead right there.

But there's an exception the pros know: if the ball has already passed a fielder (not the pitcher) and no other fielder can catch it, and then it hits you, it's not your fault: you're not out and the game goes on.
Was the ball coming 'clean' at you? Out.
Had it already passed the defense? Keep playing.

1.q: The batted ball hits your foot coming straight off the bat, without touching any fielder. What happens?
1.ko: Ball straight at the runner: out.

opts.a: You're out and the ball is dead

2.q: The ball rolled past the shortstop, nobody can play it, and then it brushes the runner. What happens?
2.ko: It had already passed a fielder: not the runner's fault.

opts.a: It's not an out: play goes on

3.q: If the batted ball hits the runner, it is always an out, with no exception
3.ko: False: if it already passed a fielder, play goes on.

4.q: Which fielder does NOT count as "already passed" if the ball goes by him?
4.ok: Correct! The pitcher doesn't count for the exception.
4.ko: If it only passed the pitcher, the runner is still out if it hits him.

opts.a: The pitcher

5.q: The ball hit the runner before any fielder touched it. What does the umpire call?
5.ok: Out! Dead ball at that moment.
5.ko: Straight at the runner: out and everything stops.

opts.a: Out! And dead ball

6.q: The ball already passed the second baseman and keeps rolling into the outfield. Tap where the play is still alive
6.ok: Good! The ball is still alive there.
6.ko: It passed the fielder: the play goes on toward the outfield.

7.4.title: Don't pass the runner ahead: the line
7.4.objective: Learn that runners are a line: you can never pass the runner ahead of you; passing another runner is an out for the one who passes.
demo: Think of a line at the store: nobody cuts in.
On the bases it's the same: the runners are a line, nobody gets ahead.
If the runner ahead stopped and you come running and pass him, you're the out, the one who passed.
That is why the runner behind always has to watch the runner ahead: if he stops, you stop too or go back.
One line, in order, no cutting in.

1.q: What happens if you pass the runner ahead of you?
1.ko: Nobody gets ahead in line: the one who passes is out.

opts.a: You're out, the one who passed

2.q: Runners can pass each other if one is faster
2.ko: False: not even the fastest cuts in.

3.q: The runner ahead stopped at third and you are coming from second at full speed. What do you do?
3.ko: The runner ahead sets your speed.

opts.a: I stop or go back to second
opts.b: I pass him and keep going home

4.q: There are runners on first and second. Tap the runner ahead, the one who leads the line
4.ok: Good! He is ahead.
4.ko: The runner on second leads the line.

5.q: You passed your teammate who had stopped between bases. What does the umpire call for you?
5.ko: Passing a runner is an out.

opts.a: Out!

6.q: Which picture shows the right line?
6.ok: Correct! In line and in order.
6.ko: The line always stays.

opts.a: Two runners in order, not passing

7.5.title: When to run: it depends on the outs
7.5.objective: Learn to run by reading the outs: with two outs you run on contact with any fair ball; with fewer than two outs and a fly ball, first you have to see if it's caught.
demo: You don't always run the same way: it depends on the outs.
With two outs, run at the crack of the bat: if they catch the ball, the inning is over anyway, so you lose nothing by running all out from the hit.
With fewer than two outs it's different: if there's a fly ball, first see if they catch it, because if you run and they catch it, they can double you off at your base.
How many outs are there? You ask that before every pitch.

1.q: With two outs, as soon as the batter makes contact on a fair ball, the runner must:
1.ok: That's it! With two outs there is nothing to protect.
1.ko: Two outs: run on contact.

opts.a: Run all out from contact

2.q: With one out and a fly ball to the outfield, the runner must first:
2.ok: Correct! There might be a tag up.
2.ko: Without two outs, you watch the fly ball first.

opts.a: See if it is caught before taking off

3.q: With two outs, if they catch the fly ball, the inning ends anyway even if the runner stayed
3.ko: True: the catch is the third out anyway.

4.q: With two outs you ran, you scored, but the outfielder caught the fly ball a second earlier. What happens to your run?
4.ok: Exactly! The third out rules.
4.ko: If the catch came first, the run doesn't count.

opts.a: It doesn't count: the catch was the third out

5.q: With two outs and a runner on second, a ground ball goes into the outfield. Tap how far the runner should try to get
5.ok: Good! With two outs he goes for the run.
5.ko: Two outs: from second, go score.

6.q: Before every pitch, the smart runner asks:
6.ok: That's it! It all depends on the outs.
6.ko: The outs decide how you run.

opts.a: How many outs are there?

8.1.title: Hit or error
8.1.objective: Tell apart, with simple examples: a hit (you get there with your good batted ball, without the defense failing) from an error (you get there or move up because the defense messed up a normal play).
demo: You reached first and the scorer has to decide: was it a hit or an error?
If your batted ball went through clean, without anyone failing, it's a hit, and you earned it.
If the fielder dropped an easy ball, or threw very badly on a normal play, it's an error: you got there with help from the defense.
The scorer asks just one question: would a normal fielder have made that play?
If yes and he failed: error. If your batted ball was impossible: hit.

1.q: Your batted ball went between two fielders who never touched it and you got there safely. Hit or error?
1.ko: No failure by the defense: hit.

opts.a: Hit

2.q: The outfielder dropped a very high, easy fly ball and you reached second. Hit or error?
2.ok: Correct! It was a normal play.
2.ko: An easy ball dropped: error.

opts.a: Error

3.q: A very wild throw that lets the batter reach can be an error
3.ok: Good! A bad throw is also an error.
3.ko: True: the bad throw counts as an error.

4.q: Which picture shows an error?
4.ok: That's it! A failure on a normal play.
4.ko: That drop is the classic error.

opts.a: A fielder dropping an easy fly ball
opts.b: A ball going clean into the outfield
opts.c: A home run over the fence

5.q: The scorer asks: the ball was hit really hard, hit the shortstop's glove and kept going. Hit or error?
5.ok: Correct! An impossible play isn't an error.
5.ko: If not even an expert could make it, it's a hit.

opts.a: Hit: it was too hard

6.q: The scorer's question is:
6.ok: That's it! That's how it's decided.
6.ko: That question separates a hit from an error.

opts.a: Would a normal fielder have made the play?

8.2.title: Run batted in
8.2.objective: Understand the run batted in (RBI): when your hit, your walk with the bases loaded or your sacrifice bunt or fly makes a teammate score, that run is credited to you as batted in.
demo: Behind almost every run there is someone who drove it in.
If your teammate scores thanks to your batted ball, that run is your run batted in, written RBI.
A single that brings in a teammate: one RBI.
A home run with two teammates on base: three RBI — and yes, your own run counts too.
Driving in runs is the batter's favorite job.

1.q: What is an RBI?
1.ko: RBI: a run you drove in.

opts.a: A run a teammate scores thanks to your hitting

2.q: You hit a single and your teammate scores from second. How many RBI?
2.ko: Each teammate you bring home is an RBI.

opts.a: One

3.q: On a solo home run, the batter also gets an RBI for his own run
3.ko: True: on a home run you count too.

4.q: Home run with teammates on first and second. How many RBI?
4.ok: That's it! Three runs driven in.
4.ko: Two teammates plus your run: three.

opts.a: Three: the two teammates and you

5.q: With the bases loaded you get a walk and a teammate is forced home. The scorer credits you with:
5.ok: Correct! You drove that run in too.
5.ko: A walk with the bases loaded gives an RBI.

opts.a: One RBI

6.q: Your single brings a teammate home from second. Tap the base where that teammate scores
6.ok: Good! That's where the run scores and your RBI is born.
6.ko: The run scores by touching home.

8.3.title: Reading the count: who's winning
8.3.objective: Read the count as a story: when the batter is ahead (a hitter's count, like 2-0 or 3-1) a fast pitch comes through the zone; when the pitcher is ahead (a pitcher's count, like 0-2 or 1-2) the batter has to protect. The pitch count is something else: how many pitches the pitcher has thrown, and it only matters for taking care of his arm.
demo: The count tells a story: who's winning the battle.
If there are more balls than strikes, like two balls and no strikes, it's a hitter's count: the pitcher needs a strike and will almost surely throw his best pitch through the zone.
If there are more strikes, like no balls and two strikes, it's a pitcher's count: the batter has to protect the zone and battle every pitch.
And careful, don't mix it up: the pitch count is not this count.
The pitch count is how many pitches the pitcher has thrown in the game, and it's for taking care of his arm, as you'll see in Level 11.

1.q: A 3-1 count, ahead in balls. It is a count for the:
1.ok: That's it! The batter is ahead.
1.ko: More balls: a hitter's count.

opts.a: Batter (hitter's count)

2.q: A 0-2 count, no balls and two strikes. It is a count for the:
2.ok: Correct! The batter is in a tough spot.
2.ko: Two strikes: the pitcher is ahead.

opts.a: Pitcher (pitcher's count)

3.q: The pitch count and the count of the at-bat (balls and strikes) are the same thing
3.ok: Good! They are two different things.
3.ko: False: the pitch count counts the pitches of the whole game.

4.q: In a hitter's count, the pitcher will almost surely:
4.ok: Correct! He needs a strike.
4.ko: Batter ahead: the pitch comes through the zone.

opts.a: Go for the zone with his best pitch

5.q: With two strikes against him, the smart batter:
5.ko: With two strikes you protect, you don't pick.

opts.a: Protects the zone: also swings at what is close
opts.b: Only swings at the perfect one

6.q: The scoreboard says 2 balls and 2 strikes. That count is called:
6.ok: Correct! Two and two, nobody is in charge.
6.ko: Full is 3 and 2, as you saw in Level 4.

opts.a: An even count, two and two

8.4.title: Scoring with numbers
8.4.objective: Read plays written with the Level 2 position numbers (a 6-4-3 double play), the K for a strikeout swinging and the backwards K for a strikeout looking, and the E for an error.
demo: Remember the position numbers from Level 2?
Scorers use them to write plays without words.
A 6-4-3 double play means: shortstop to second base, second base to first: two outs!
K is the strikeout letter: a regular K means the batter struck out swinging, and a backwards K means he struck out looking, without swinging.
And E is the mark for an error: E6 means an error by the shortstop.
Reading these codes is reading the game in secret.

1.q: In a 6-4-3, who gets the ball first?
1.ko: You read the chain in order: 6, 4, 3.

opts.a: The second baseman (4)

2.q: What play is a classic 6-4-3?
2.ok: That's it! Two outs written in numbers.
2.ko: 6-4-3: the double play recipe.

opts.a: A double play

3.q: The K on the scoresheet means strikeout
3.ko: True: the K is the strikeout.

4.q: E6 on the scoresheet means:
4.ok: Correct! E for error, 6 for the shortstop.
4.ko: The letter says what; the number says who.

opts.a: Error by the shortstop

5.q: Drag the ball along the 6-4-3 chain: shortstop, second base, first base
5.ko: From 6 to 4 and from 4 to 3.

6.q: The scoresheet shows a backwards K for a batter. That means he struck out:
6.ok: That's it! A backwards K means he struck out looking.
6.ko: Regular K: swinging. Backwards K: looking.

opts.a: Swinging

8.5.title: The full scoreboard
8.5.objective: Read the full scoreboard: runs (R), hits (H) and errors (E) for each team, and the runs in each inning, without calculating anything else.
demo: The scoreboard is the game's newspaper.
The innings go across the top, and each team puts its runs inning by inning.
At the end there are three big numbers: R, runs; H, hits; and E, errors.
A team can have more hits and lose: runs win, not hits.
And an error on the scoreboard is nobody's shame: it's information, it tells what happened.
Always read in this order: runs, hits, errors.

1.q: On the scoreboard, R means:
1.ko: The R is what wins the game.

opts.a: Runs

2.q: The H on the scoreboard counts:
2.ko: Hits: each team's good batted balls.

opts.a: Each team's hits

3.q: The team with more hits wins even if it has fewer runs
3.ko: False: runs rule, not hits.

4.q: The E on the scoreboard counts:
4.ok: That's it! E for errors.
4.ko: Errors: failures on normal plays.

opts.a: Each team's errors

5.q: A scoreboard says 5 R, 8 H, 1 E against 3 R, 9 H, 0 E. Who won?
5.ko: More hits isn't always winning.

opts.a: The one with 5 runs, even with fewer hits

6.q: On a drawn scoreboard, tap the runs column (R) of the top team
6.ko: R: the number that decides the game.
6.answer: The R (runs) of the first row

9.1.title: The stolen base
9.1.objective: Understand the stolen base: moving up to the next base during the pitch, with no batted ball, and that whether stealing is allowed — and from what age — depends on the league and the age group.
demo: Stealing a base is moving up to the next one while the pitcher pitches, without a batted ball.
That's called a stolen base.
You take off when the pitcher starts his motion toward home, and it's a race between you, the catcher's throw and the base waiting for you.
But listen to the most important part: you can't steal in every kids' league, and each league decides from what age.
Ask your coach if your league has steals: he has the answer for your league.

1.q: What is stealing a base?
1.ko: Stealing: you move up with the pitch, not with a hit.

opts.a: Moving up during the pitch, with no batted ball
opts.b: Taking the base home with you

2.q: In every kids' league you can steal from any age
2.ko: False: ask your coach about your league.

3.q: When does the stealing runner take off?
3.ko: The steal starts with the pitch.

opts.a: When the pitcher starts his motion or releases the ball toward home

4.q: You reached second before the fielder's tag. What does the umpire call?
4.ok: Safe! Steal made.
4.ko: You got there first: stolen base.

opts.a: Safe! Stolen base

5.q: You're stealing from first. Tap the base you want to steal
5.ok: Good! Second is the most stolen.
5.ko: The classic steal is to second.

6.q: If your league doesn't allow steals yet, what do you do?
6.ok: That's it! Each league has its time.
6.ko: Your league's rules are always respected.

opts.a: I respect my league's rule and ask the coach

9.2.title: Taking a lead
9.2.objective: Understand taking a lead: moving a few steps away from the base to shorten the path, getting back fast if the pitcher looks, and that many kids' leagues don't allow leads until the ball crosses home.
demo: Before stealing, the runner takes a lead: a few little steps away from his base to be closer to the next one.
That's called taking a lead.
But the lead is risky: you're off your safe spot.
If the pitcher turns and throws to your base, you have to fly back.
And careful: in many leagues for young kids you can't take a lead until the pitch goes past home.
Can you take a lead in your league? Ask your coach before you do it.

1.q: What is taking a lead off the base?
1.ko: Taking a lead shortens your path.

opts.a: Moving a few steps away from the base to get ready to advance
opts.c: Pulling the base off the ground

2.q: Taking too big a lead is free: nothing ever happens
2.ok: Good! Far from your base there's danger.
2.ko: False: off the base, a good throw can get you out.

3.q: You've taken a lead and the pitcher turns toward your base. What do you do?
3.ok: Correct! Back to your safe spot.
3.ko: Pitcher looking: go back right away.

opts.a: I run back to my base

4.q: Tap where a runner leading off first is: between which two bases
4.ok: Good! That's where the leading runner floats.
4.ko: With a lead, you're between two bases, off your safe spot.

5.q: In many kids' leagues, the runner can only take a lead:
5.ok: That's it! That's why you ask the coach.
5.ko: Each league sets its moment for leads.

opts.a: When the pitch goes past home
opts.b: From the moment he reaches the base

6.q: You took a big lead and the pitcher's throw got to first before you got back. What is the call?
6.ok: Out! The lead costs you if you get careless.
6.ko: Getting back late from a lead is an out.

opts.a: Out!

9.3.title: The pickoff
9.3.objective: Understand the pickoff: the pitcher (or the catcher) throws by surprise to a base to try to get the runner who took a lead out, and why the runner has to get back touching the base.
demo: The pitcher plays too.
If you take a big lead, he can turn by surprise and throw to your base: that's a pickoff, a throw to catch you off your base.
If his throw gets there and the fielder tags you before you get back, you are out.
That's why the runner with a lead is always ready: one eye on the pitcher and his body set to dive back.
And if the ball goes far on a bad throw, then yes, run!

1.q: What is a pickoff?
1.ko: The pitcher defends his base with that throw.

opts.a: A surprise throw by the pitcher to a base to get the runner with a lead out

2.q: On a pickoff, if you get back to your base before the tag, you are safe
2.ok: Good! Your base keeps you safe.
2.ko: True: getting there first is safe.

3.q: The pickoff throw gets away far from the first baseman. As the runner, what do you do?
3.ok: Correct! Ball far away: take advantage.
3.ko: A bad pickoff throw gives away a base.

opts.a: I run to the next base!
opts.c: I go back to the dugout

4.q: The pitcher throws a pickoff to first. Tap the base where the fielder waits for the throw to tag you
4.ok: Good! That's where the pickoff is decided.
4.ko: First receives the surprise throw.

5.q: The pickoff throw got there and you were tagged one step before getting back to the base. What is the call?
5.ko: Tagged off your base: out.

opts.a: Out!

6.q: The best antidote against the pickoff is:
6.ko: Take a lead with your head, not with greed.

opts.a: A short lead and getting back fast

9.4.title: The balk: the trick that doesn't count
9.4.objective: Understand the balk in simple words: an illegal move by the pitcher with runners on base — starting to pitch and stopping, or faking a throw without letting go of the ball — punished with one base for each runner; and that in many kids' leagues the balk isn't called or is taught with a warning first.
demo: The pitcher can trick you with his eyes, but not with his body.
If, with runners on base, he starts his pitching motion and stops, or acts like he's throwing to a base and doesn't let go of the ball, he committed a balk.
The penalty is fair: each runner moves up one base for free.
It's like moving a game piece out of turn: it doesn't count.
And listen: in many kids' leagues the balk isn't called, or the umpire warns first to teach.
Are balks called in your league? Your coach knows.

1.q: What is a balk?
1.ko: An illegal move by the pitcher: that's a balk.

opts.a: An illegal move by the pitcher with runners on base

2.q: What is the penalty for a balk?
2.ok: Correct! A free base per runner.
2.ko: Balk: everybody moves up one.

opts.a: Each runner moves up one base

3.q: A balk can only be called if there are runners on base
3.ko: True: with no runners, that move isn't punished that way.

4.q: Which picture shows a balk?
4.ok: That's it! Starting and stopping: balk.
4.ko: Stopping halfway through the motion is the classic balk.

opts.a: The pitcher starts to pitch and stops halfway
opts.b: The pitcher pitches normally to home
opts.c: The pitcher makes a legal, complete pickoff

5.q: The pitcher faked a throw to first and kept the ball, with a runner on first. What does the umpire call?
5.ok: Balk! And the runner moves up.
5.ko: Faking without letting go: balk and one base.

opts.a: Balk! Runner to second

6.q: In your kids' league, maybe the balk:
6.ok: Correct! Each league handles it its own way.
6.ko: With kids, many leagues teach before punishing.

opts.a: Isn't called yet, or they warn first: ask your coach

9.5.title: Wild pitch and passed ball
9.5.objective: Tell apart: a wild pitch is a pitch so bad the catcher can't catch or block it (the pitcher's fault); a passed ball is a catchable ball that gets away from the catcher (the catcher's fault). In both, runners can advance at their own risk.
demo: Sometimes the ball gets away behind the catcher and the runners run.
Whose fault was it?
If the pitch was so bad — very high, very low or very far — that the catcher had no way to catch it, it's a wild pitch: the pitcher's fault.
If the ball was normal and catchable and the catcher let it get away, it's a passed ball: the catcher's fault.
Different faults, same hurry: the runners can try to move up, and the catcher has to get the ball back fast.

1.q: The pitch goes over the catcher's head, impossible to catch. It is:
1.ko: Impossible ball: wild pitch.

opts.a: Wild pitch

2.q: The ball arrives normally at the glove and gets away from the catcher. It is:
2.ok: Correct! It was catchable: passed ball.
2.ko: Catchable and got away: passed ball.

opts.a: Passed ball

3.q: On a wild pitch or a passed ball, the runners can advance if they dare
3.ko: True: loose ball, run carefully.

4.q: The difference between a wild pitch and a passed ball is:
4.ok: That's it! That's how the scorer decides.
4.ko: Same escape, different faults.

opts.a: Whose fault it is: the pitcher's or the catcher's

5.q: The ball got away to the back and the runner from third scored. That play is NOT scored as:
5.ok: Correct! Moving up on a ball that got away isn't a steal.
5.ko: A steal happens during the pitch, not because of the escape.

opts.a: Stolen base

6.q: The ball that got away rolled all the way to the back, behind home. Tap where the catcher has to run to get it
6.ko: The loose ball is behind home.

10.1.title: Dropped third strike
10.1.objective: Understand the dropped third strike: if the catcher doesn't catch the third strike cleanly, the batter can run to first when the rule applies — first base open, or first occupied with two outs — and that in many kids' leagues this rule doesn't exist yet.
demo: The batter struck out… or did he?
If the catcher doesn't catch the third strike cleanly — he drops it or it bounces first — and the rule applies, the batter can run to first!
It's called the dropped third strike.
It applies when first base is open, or when there are two outs even if first is occupied.
The catcher has to tag him with the ball or throw to first.
And watch out for your league: in many leagues for young kids this rule isn't used: a strikeout is a strikeout, period.
Ask your coach if the batter can run in your league.

1.q: What is the dropped third strike?
1.ko: Third strike without a clean catch: run, if the rule applies.

opts.a: The catcher doesn't catch the third strike cleanly and the batter can run to first
opts.b: A strike that always falls to the ground before the batter

2.q: With first base open and one out, the third strike gets away from the catcher. The batter must:
2.ko: The rule gives you that chance.

opts.a: Run to first

3.q: With first occupied and fewer than two outs, the batter can also run on a dropped third strike
3.ok: Good! With first occupied it only applies with two outs.
3.ko: False: first occupied closes the door, except with two outs.

4.q: Two outs and first occupied, dropped third strike. The batter:
4.ok: That's it! With two outs the door opens.
4.ko: Two outs: even if first is occupied, he can run.

opts.a: Yes, can run to first

5.q: The catcher caught the third strike cleanly. What does the umpire call?
5.ok: Out! Clean catch, no running to first.
5.ko: If the catcher catches it cleanly, the strikeout is final.

opts.a: Out! Complete strikeout

6.q: In your kids' league, the first thing you need to know about this rule is:
6.ok: Correct! Many small leagues don't use it.
6.ko: League rule: coach first.

opts.a: If my league uses it at my age: ask your coach
opts.b: That it always counts everywhere in the world

10.2.title: Infield fly: the out that protects
10.2.objective: Understand the infield fly and why: with runners on first and second (or the bases loaded) and fewer than two outs, an easy fly ball to the infield is an automatic out for the batter, so the defense doesn't drop it on purpose to make a sneaky double play.
demo: Listen to the why, and you'll never forget it.
Runners on first and second, an easy fly ball to the infield.
If the defense drops it on purpose, the runners are trapped: they don't know whether to run or stay, and the defense would get an easy double play.
To protect the runners there is the infield fly: the umpire calls "infield fly, batter out" as soon as he sees it's an easy infield fly ball, with fewer than two outs.
The batter is out even if the ball falls, and the runners can move up at their own risk, as with any fly ball.
The rule punishes the trick, not the batter.

1.q: Why does the infield fly exist?
1.ok: That's it! It protects the runners.
1.ko: The rule is a shield against the trick.

opts.a: So the defense doesn't drop an easy fly ball on purpose to make a sneaky double play

2.q: The infield fly is called with runners on:
2.ok: Correct! Those bases and those outs.
2.ko: First and second, fewer than two outs: that's where the rule lives.

opts.a: First and second (or bases loaded) and fewer than two outs

3.q: The infield fly is also called with two outs
3.ok: Good! With two outs it isn't needed.
3.ko: False: with two outs the trick doesn't work, it isn't called.

4.q: Easy fly ball to the shortstop with runners on first and second and one out. The umpire calls:
4.ok: That's it! Out before it falls.
4.ko: The call comes with the ball in the air.

opts.a: "Infield fly! Batter out"

5.q: If the infield fly ball falls to the ground without anyone catching it, the batter:
5.ok: Correct! The out was already called.
5.ko: Whether it falls or not: batter out.

opts.a: Is out anyway

6.q: Which fly ball can be an infield fly?
6.ok: That's it! Easy and in the infield.
6.ko: It has to be a fly ball an infielder catches without hurrying.

opts.a: An easy, high fly ball over the infield
opts.b: A hard line drive to the outfield
opts.c: A deep fly ball to the wall

10.3.title: Live ball and dead ball
10.3.objective: Tell apart a live ball (you can run and make outs) from a dead ball (everything stops: a foul is the everyday example, also time requested and granted, and a pitch that hits the batter).
demo: The ball has two states, like a traffic light.
Live ball: the light is green, you can run, throw and make outs.
Dead ball: red light, everything stops and nobody can move up or be put out.
A foul is a dead ball.
When the umpire grants time, too.
And when a pitch hits the batter, the ball goes dead that very instant.
Learn the traffic light: green, play; red, freeze.

1.q: With a live ball, players can:
1.ko: Live ball: the game goes on.

opts.a: Run, throw and make outs

2.q: A foul ball turns the ball into:
2.ko: Foul: red light.

opts.a: Dead ball

3.q: With a dead ball, a runner can move up to the next base
3.ok: Good! Nobody moves on a red light.
3.ko: False: dead ball, everyone freezes.

4.q: You ask for time and the umpire grants it by raising his hands. The ball is:
4.ok: Correct! Time granted: dead ball.
4.ko: With the umpire's time, everything stops.

opts.a: Dead

5.q: The pitch hits the batter. At that instant the ball:
5.ok: That's it! Hit by the pitch: dead ball.
5.ko: When the pitch hits the batter, the play stops right away.

opts.a: Goes dead: nobody can move up on that play

6.q: The runner was halfway when foul was called. Tap where he has to go back with the dead ball
6.ok: Good! On a dead ball you go back.
6.ko: Red light: everyone to their base.

10.4.title: Interference and obstruction
10.4.objective: Tell apart in simple words: interference is when the batting team gets in the way of a fielder who is playing the ball; obstruction is when a fielder without the ball blocks a runner's path.
demo: Two long words for a short idea: don't get in the way and don't block.
If your team is batting and someone gets in the way of a fielder about to play the ball, that's interference: whoever got in the way pays, almost always with an out.
If a fielder without the ball stands in the way and blocks a runner, that's obstruction: the defense pays, and the runner moves up protected.
Did the batting team get in the way? Interference.
Did a fielder without the ball block? Obstruction.

1.q: A runner crashes into the shortstop just as he is about to catch a ground ball. It is:
1.ok: Correct! He got in the way of the one playing the ball.
1.ko: The offense got in the way: interference.

opts.a: The runner's interference

2.q: The first baseman, without the ball, stands on the line and blocks the runner rounding the base. It is:
2.ok: That's it! A fielder without the ball blocking.
2.ko: Blocking without the ball: obstruction.

opts.a: Obstruction

3.q: If the fielder has the ball, he can be in the path to tag the runner
3.ok: Good! With the ball, the fielder is playing.
3.ko: True: with the ball he can go for the tag.

4.q: The batter interfered with the catcher as he tried to throw. The umpire declares:
4.ok: Correct! Whoever gets in the way pays.
4.ko: Interference by the offense: out.

opts.a: Out for interference

5.q: The quick way to tell them apart is to ask:
5.ko: Offense gets in the way: interference. Defense blocks: obstruction.

opts.a: Who got in the way: the offense or a fielder without the ball?

6.q: Tap the player committing obstruction: the fielder standing without the ball in the path between first and second
6.ok: Good! He blocks without playing the ball.
6.ko: Without the ball and in the path: obstruction.
6.answer: The fielder without the ball in the path

10.5.title: Missing a base: the appeal
10.5.objective: Understand that if a runner misses a base (or leaves early on a tag up), the defense can appeal: with the ball live, touch the base or the runner and show the mistake to the umpire; if the appeal succeeds, it's an out.
demo: Remember Level 1: you have to touch every base.
If a runner skips one — or left before the catch on a tag up — the umpire doesn't call it on his own.
The defense has to appeal: with the ball live, a fielder touches the missed base, or the runner, and clearly shows the umpire what happened.
If the umpire saw it and agrees: out on appeal.
No appeal, no penalty.
The defense has to be wide awake too.

1.q: What is an appeal?
1.ko: Appealing is showing the mistake with the ball in play.

opts.a: The defense shows the umpire a missed base, touching the base or the runner with the ball live

2.q: If a runner misses a base and nobody appeals, the game goes on without a penalty
2.ko: True: the defense has to ask for it.

3.q: The runner stepped wrong and went right past second on his way. The defense appeals by touching:
3.ok: Correct! The base that was missed.
3.ko: You appeal at the forgotten base.

opts.a: Second base with the ball

4.q: The defense appealed correctly and the umpire saw the runner never touched second. He calls:
4.ok: Out! Appeal won.
4.ko: Missed base plus appeal: out.

opts.a: Out!

5.q: A runner scored but left before the catch on a tag up. The defense can:
5.ok: That's it! Leaving early can be appealed too.
5.ko: A tag up done wrong: appeal.

opts.a: Appeal by touching his starting base with the ball

6.q: The runner skipped third on the way home. Tap the base where the defense has to appeal
6.ok: Good! That's where the mistake is shown.
6.ko: The appeal lives at the forgotten base.

11.1.title: The pitcher's rubber
