11.1.objective: Understand that the pitcher pitches with his foot on the mound's rubber, that every pitch starts there, and that the distance from the mound to home changes with age and league.
demo: At the top of the mound there's a little white board: the rubber.
The pitcher pitches with one foot on it: everything starts there.
With that foot on the rubber, the pitcher looks at the catcher, gets the sign and pitches.
Pay attention to this big truth: the distance from the rubber to home isn't the same for everyone.
In kids' leagues it's shorter and it grows with age.
What is it in your league? Your field measures it, and your coach knows it.

1.q: What is the pitcher's rubber?
1.ko: Every pitch starts from the rubber.

opts.a: The little white board on the mound where the pitcher puts his foot

2.q: The distance from the rubber to home is the same at every age
2.ok: Good! It changes with age and league.
2.ko: False: for kids it's shorter.

3.q: When pitching, the pitcher has to start:
3.ko: The rubber is his starting point.

opts.a: With one foot on the rubber

4.q: Tap the rubber: the little board at the top of the mound
4.ok: Good! That's where the rubber is.
4.ko: In the center of the diamond, on top of the mound.

5.q: The pitcher gets the sign looking at the catcher, standing on the rubber. That is the start of:
5.ok: Correct! Every pitch is born there.
5.ko: Sign, rubber and pitch: the full routine.

opts.a: Every pitch

6.q: If you want to know the exact distance of your mound, you should:
6.ok: That's it! It depends on your league and your age.
6.ko: Don't copy the grown-ups' numbers.

opts.a: Ask your coach or look at your league's rule

11.2.title: Windup and set: the two ways to pitch
11.2.objective: Tell apart the windup (full motion, step back and arms up, used mostly with no runners) from the set or stretch (short motion from a pause, used with runners to keep them close).
demo: The pitcher has two ways to start.
With no runners, he can use the windup: the full, calm motion, with his step and his arms going up, like gathering momentum with his whole body.

With runners on base he uses the set, also called the stretch: he gets in position, makes a still pause facing home — that pause is required — and pitches quick and short, to give the runner less of an edge.
Windup to pitch comfortably; set to watch the bases.

1.q: What is the windup?
1.ko: Windup: the whole body takes part.

opts.a: The full pitching motion, with a step and momentum

2.q: With runners on base, the pitcher usually pitches from:
2.ok: Correct! Set to watch the bases.
2.ko: With runners, a short motion.

opts.a: The set (stretch), short and with a pause

3.q: In the set, the pitcher must make a still pause before pitching home
3.ok: Good! The pause is part of the rule.
3.ko: True: with no pause in the set, it can be a balk.

4.q: Which picture shows the set?
4.ok: That's it! Still and sideways: set.
4.ko: You recognize the set by the pause.

opts.a: The pitcher still, sideways, looking, before a short pitch
opts.b: The pitcher with his arms way up taking a step back

5.q: From the set, without making his pause and with a runner on base, the pitcher hurries a pitch home. The umpire can call:
5.ko: Remember Level 9: tricking with the body doesn't count.

opts.a: Balk: he didn't make the set pause

6.q: The set helps the pitcher:
6.ok: That's it! Less of an edge for the steal.
6.ko: Short motion, less time stolen.

opts.a: Watch the runners and pitch home faster

11.3.title: Fastball and changeup: the first pitches
11.3.objective: Learn that a kid's first pitches are the fastball and the changeup (which looks like a fastball but arrives slower), and that curveballs aren't for young arms: only when the coach decides, with the body ready.
demo: A young pitcher needs only two pitches, done well.
First the fastball: your straight pitch, with control.
Then the changeup: it comes out just like the fastball, with the same arm motion, but it arrives slower and fools the batter who has already swung.
And curveballs? Listen carefully: curveballs aren't for you yet.
Throwing curveballs with a growing arm can hurt it.
Fastball and changeup first, always.
Curveballs come later, only when your coach decides and your body is ready.

1.q: What are the first two pitches a young pitcher learns?
1.ko: Those two, done well, are enough.

opts.a: Fastball and changeup

2.q: What makes the changeup special?
2.ok: Correct! It fools you with speed.
2.ko: Same arm, slower ball.

opts.a: It looks like a fastball but arrives slower

3.q: A kid should practice curveballs all day to be a good pitcher
3.ko: False: your growing arm comes first.

4.q: Who decides when a young player can start with curveballs?
4.ok: That's it! Calmly and with permission.
4.ko: Curveballs only with the coach's decision.

opts.a: The coach, when the body is ready
opts.b: The kid alone, whenever he wants

5.q: The batter swung way too early at a changeup that came floating in. The umpire calls:
5.ok: Strike! The changeup did its job.
5.ko: It came slow and the swing went by first.

opts.a: Strike! The changeup fooled him

6.q: Which grip and pitch do you learn first?
6.ko: The fastball is the base of every pitcher.

opts.a: The fastball, holding the ball with your fingers across the seams

11.4.title: Taking care of your arm
11.4.objective: Learn that the arm is cared for with rules: there is a maximum number of pitches and rest days that depend on age and league (with no fixed number in this lesson), you warm up before pitching, and if your arm or elbow hurts, you stop and tell an adult.
demo: Your arm is your treasure, and treasures are protected with rules.
That's why there's the pitch count — you already met it in Level 8 — and rest days: your league sets a maximum number of pitches for your age, and then says to rest.
Those numbers change with age and with league, so you won't see any here: ask your coach which ones are yours and always respect them.
Warm up before pitching, don't pitch every day, and listen to the golden rule: if your arm or elbow hurts, you stop and tell an adult.
No pitching through pain.
A game isn't worth an arm.

1.q: If your arm or elbow hurts while pitching, the right thing is to:
1.ok: That's it! That's the golden rule.
1.ko: Pain is always a signal to stop.

opts.a: Stop and tell an adult
opts.c: Pitch with the other arm without saying anything

2.q: The maximum number of pitches and the rest are the same for every age and league
2.ok: Good! They change with age and league.
2.ko: False: that's why your league and your coach set them.

3.q: What is the pitch count for?
3.ko: Every pitch counts for your arm.

opts.a: To not go over the maximum for your age and to take care of your arm

4.q: Before pitching in a game or practice, the pitcher must:
4.ok: That's it! A cold arm gets hurt.
4.ko: Warming up is part of pitching.

opts.a: Warm up the arm throwing softly and gradually
opts.b: Throw as hard as possible from the first ball

5.q: The coach comes out to talk with his pitcher, who has already thrown a lot. Most likely what comes is:
5.ok: Correct! Taking care is also managing.
5.ko: The count rules: time to rest.

opts.a: A pitching change to take care of him

6.q: Which picture shows taking care of your arm?
6.ok: That's it! Resting is part of the plan.
6.ko: Rest trains too: it protects.

opts.a: A pitcher resting in the dugout after his outing
opts.b: A pitcher throwing alone every day
opts.c: A pitcher throwing with a bandaged arm and pain

11.5.title: The relief pitcher
11.5.objective: Understand relief pitching: when a pitcher leaves, another comes in from the bullpen; the one who opens the game is the starter and the one who comes in later is the reliever, and changing pitchers is also a way of taking care of arms.
demo: No arm pitches the whole game, much less a young arm.
The pitcher who starts is called the starter.

When he leaves — because of his count, because he is tired or for strategy — the relief comes in: the reliever, who was warming up in the bullpen, that space in the back where pitchers practice before coming in.
The reliever comes in with the game already going and has to be ready from his first pitch.
Changing pitchers isn't a punishment: it's taking care of the arm and giving the team a fresh arm.

1.q: What is a reliever?
1.ok: That's it! He comes in with the game going.
1.ko: Relief: a new arm on the mound.

opts.a: The pitcher who comes in during the game to replace another

2.q: The pitcher who opens the game is called:
2.ko: The first one on the mound is the starter.

opts.a: Starter

3.q: The reliever warms up in the bullpen before coming in
3.ko: True: the bullpen is his warm-up room.

4.q: A pitcher leaves the game, partly, because:
4.ok: That's it! Taking care of the arm comes first.
4.ko: The pitch count also decides relief.

opts.a: His pitch count reached the maximum for his age and league

5.q: A new pitcher comes in mid-inning. Before going on, the umpire allows him:
5.ok: Correct! He comes in and warms up a bit right there.
5.ko: Every new pitcher warms up before playing.

opts.a: A few warm-up pitches on the mound

6.q: Tap the bullpen: the area, usually behind the outfield or to one side, where relievers warm up
6.ok: Good! That's where they wait, ready.
6.ko: Bullpen: the relievers' home.

12.1.title: Where to throw the ball
12.1.objective: Think before every pitch about where the ball will go depending on the runners and the outs, looking first to stop the lead runner and taking the sure out when the hard throw can't be made.
demo: You've got the ball in your glove and everyone is running.
Where do you throw it?
The All Star answers before the ball is hit: before every pitch he asks himself, if it's hit to me, what do I do?
It's almost always best to stop the lead runner, the one closest to scoring.
But a sure out is worth more than an impossible throw: if the long throw can't be made, make sure of the out at first.
Thinking ahead: that's what separates a player from an All Star.

1.q: When should you think about where you will throw the ball?
1.ok: That's it! The play is thought out beforehand.
1.ko: The All Star arrives with the plan ready.

opts.a: Before every pitch
opts.b: When you already have it in your glove

2.q: No runners, you field a ground ball. Where do you throw?
2.ok: Correct! The out is at first.
2.ko: No runners: first rules.

opts.a: To first

3.q: A sure out is better than trying an impossible throw and getting none
3.ok: Yes! Make sure of the out.
3.ko: True: a real out is worth more than a dream.

4.q: Runner on first, easy ground ball to the shortstop with time. Tap the base where you stop the lead runner
4.ok: Good! That's where you stop the leader.
4.ko: The lead runner is stopped at second.

5.q: Which runner is it best to stop first?
5.ok: Correct! He's the closest to scoring.
5.ko: The leader of the line is the biggest danger.

opts.a: The lead runner

6.q: Two outs and a runner on first, ground ball to the second baseman. The easiest play is:
6.ok: That's it! One out and it's over.
6.ko: With two outs, the closest out wins.

opts.a: Throw to first or step on second: one out ends the inning

12.2.title: The cutoff man
12.2.objective: Understand the cutoff: on long throws from the outfield, an infielder gets in the path, receives the throw and relays it quickly to whatever base is needed.
demo: The outfield is far away, and a direct throw home can arrive weak or off target.
That's why there's the cutoff man: an infielder gets in the path, raises his arms so the outfielder sees him, receives the throw and spins fast to throw wherever it's needed.
Two short, strong throws beat one long, weak one.
The cutoff man is the defense's fast messenger.

1.q: What does the cutoff man do?
1.ko: Cutoff: the bridge for long throws.

opts.a: Receives the outfielder's throw and relays it to whatever base is needed

2.q: Why is a cutoff man used?
2.ko: Short throws: fewer mistakes.

opts.a: Because two short throws arrive better than one long, weak one

3.q: Drag the ball along its path: center fielder, cutoff man, home
3.ko: From the outfield to the cutoff, from the cutoff to home.

4.q: The cutoff man raises his arms so the outfielder knows who to throw to
4.ok: Yes! He has to be easy to see.
4.ko: True: arms up, a clear target.

5.q: What's the name of the infielder who relays the outfielder's throw?
5.ko: That's the cutoff man.

opts.a: Cutoff

6.q: The cutoff man is usually:
6.ok: Correct! Shortstop or second baseman, depending on the throw.
6.ko: The infield relays for the outfield.

opts.a: An infielder

12.3.title: Covering and backing up
12.3.objective: Learn that on every play everyone moves: if a fielder goes after the ball, another covers his base, and behind every base receiving a throw there should be a back up in case the ball gets away.
demo: On defense nobody stands still watching.
If the first baseman goes far to get a ground ball, the pitcher runs to cover first.
And when there is a throw to a base, another fielder runs to get behind that base to back up: if the ball gets away, he stops it and saves a base.
Covering is filling the base that was left empty; backing up is being the net behind the throw.
On every play, every player has a job.

1.q: The first baseman went far for a ground ball. Who covers first?
1.ko: First is empty: the pitcher fills it.

opts.a: The pitcher

2.q: What is backing up?
2.ok: Correct! The net behind the throw.
2.ko: Backing up saves bases.

opts.a: Getting behind the base receiving a throw, in case the ball gets away

3.q: On defense only the player catching the ball moves
3.ko: False: every play moves all nine.

4.q: The catcher throws to second on a steal attempt. Tap the outfielder backing up behind second
4.ok: That's it! The center fielder backs up second.
4.ko: Behind second lives the center fielder.

5.q: What is backing up for?
5.ok: Correct! A mistake doesn't turn into a disaster.
5.ko: The net turns an escape into just a scare.

opts.a: So a ball that gets away doesn't give away extra bases

6.q: What's it called when you get behind a base in case the throw gets away?
6.ko: That's called backing up.

opts.a: Back up

12.4.title: The coach's signs and the final review
12.4.objective: Meet the first and third base coaches, who see the whole play and tell you to keep going or stop, and the team's secret signs; and review in short situations the special rules from Levels 9 and 10, only as a review.
demo: Next to first and third are the base coaches, inside their boxes.
They see the whole field and tell you whether to keep going or stop: listening to your third base coach is part of running well.
The team also has hand signs to call for a bunt or a steal: they're secret and you don't tell the other team.

And before we finish, a lightning review of what you learned in Star — a review, not a new lesson: if the pitcher fakes and doesn't let go, it's a balk; if the third strike isn't caught cleanly, the batter can run when the rule applies; and the easy fly ball with first and second occupied is an infield fly.
If you already knew it, you're ready to think like an All Star.

1.q: Where are the base coaches?
1.ko: First and third each have their coach.

opts.a: Next to first and next to third

2.q: You come running to third and your coach raises his hands for you to stop. What do you do?
2.ok: That's it! The coach sees everything.
2.ko: Hands up: stop at third.

opts.a: I stop at third

3.q: The team's signs can be told to the other team if they ask nicely
3.ko: False: the signs belong to the team.

4.q: Review: the pitcher faked a throw to first and didn't let go of the ball, with a runner on base. That was:
4.ok: Good, review done! It was a balk.
4.ko: Level 9 review: faking without letting go is a balk.

opts.a: A balk

5.q: Review: easy fly ball to the infield, runners on first and second, one out. What does the umpire call?
5.ko: Infield fly: batter out, called in the air.

opts.a: "Infield fly! Batter out"

6.q: You didn't understand a sign from the coach. The best thing is:
6.ok: Good! Asking is what an All Star does.
6.ko: Better to ask than to guess.

opts.a: Ask for time and ask

12.5.title: Sportsmanship: how an All Star behaves
12.5.objective: Close the content with the All Star's behavior: respecting the umpire's decisions, cheering on a teammate who makes a mistake, shaking hands with the other team at the end win or lose, and letting the coach talk to the umpire when there is a disagreement.
demo: An All Star isn't just the one who hits home runs.

It's the one who respects the umpire's decision even if he doesn't like it, who cheers on his teammate when he makes a mistake instead of making fun of him, and who shakes hands with the other team at the end of the game, win or lose.
That's sportsmanship.
If your team doesn't agree with a play, the one who talks to the umpire is your coach, with respect.
Playing well is trained; behaving well is too.
That's thinking — and acting — like an All Star.

1.q: The umpire calls a strike that looked like a ball to you. What does an All Star do?
1.ok: That's an All Star! The umpire decides.
1.ko: Respect and keep going: that's how you play.

opts.a: Respects the decision and keeps batting

2.q: Your teammate made an error that cost a run. What do you say to him?
2.ok: Correct! Cheering is what a team does.
2.ko: Everyone makes mistakes: the All Star lifts them up.

opts.a: "Don't worry, the next one is yours!"
opts.c: Nothing, and I get angry at him

3.q: At the end of the game you shake hands with the other team only if you won
3.ko: False: win or lose, you shake hands.

4.q: If your team doesn't agree with a decision, who talks to the umpire?
4.ok: That's it! The coach, and with respect.
4.ko: Talking is the coach's job.

opts.a: The coach, with respect

5.q: Which picture shows sportsmanship?
5.ok: Correct! Respect at the end of the game.
5.ko: The handshake line: the close of every game.

opts.a: Two teams shaking hands at the end
opts.b: A player throwing his helmet in anger
opts.c: A player making fun of the other team

6.q: What do we call respecting the umpire, your teammates and the other team?
6.ko: That word belongs to an All Star too.

opts.a: Sportsmanship

13.1.title: The catcher's gear
13.1.objective: Know the pieces of the catcher's gear (helmet, mask, chest protector, shin guards and mitt) and that they are worn complete every time you catch a pitcher, warming up too.
demo: The catcher dresses like a knight in armor, and not just for fun: he catches the fastest ball in the game.
He wears a helmet and mask for his head and face, a chest protector for his chest and shin guards for his legs.
On his hand he wears the catcher's mitt: a big, padded glove.
The golden rule: you never catch a pitcher without your full gear, not even to warm up.
Your armor is what lets you play without fear.

1.q: Why does the catcher wear so much gear?
1.ok: That's it! His armor takes care of him.
1.ko: The catcher catches every pitch: he needs protection.

opts.a: To protect himself from the fastest ball in the game

2.q: Which picture shows the catcher ready to catch?
2.ko: You never catch without a mask.

opts.a: Catcher with helmet, mask, chest protector and shin guards
opts.b: Catcher with a cap and no mask

3.q: To warm up with the pitcher, the catcher can catch without a mask
3.ok: Good! Not even to warm up.
3.ko: False: the gear is always complete, warming up too.

4.q: What is the catcher's special glove called?
4.ok: That's it! Catcher's mitt.
4.ko: It's the catcher's mitt: big and padded.

opts.a: The catcher's mitt

5.q: Drag each piece to its place: mask, chest protector, shin guards
5.ok: Perfect! Each piece in its spot.
5.ko: Mask on the face, chest protector on the chest, shin guards on the legs.

6.q: Before catching, what does the catcher check?
6.ok: That's it! The check comes first.
6.ko: Check your armor before every game.

opts.a: That his gear is complete and put on right
opts.b: That the dugout is watching him

13.2.title: Signs to the pitcher
13.2.objective: Understand that the catcher asks the pitcher for the pitch with finger signs hidden between his legs, and that in kids' leagues the coach often decides what to call.
demo: The catcher and the pitcher talk without saying a word.
Crouched down, the catcher hides his hand between his legs and shows fingers: one finger can be the fastball, two fingers the changeup.
They're called signs.
He hides them so the other team can't see them.
The pitcher looks, and if he agrees, he pitches.
In kids' leagues, the coach often passes the sign to the catcher and the catcher passes it to the pitcher.
If you didn't understand a sign, ask for time and talk: you never pitch by guessing.

1.q: What are signs for?
1.ok: That's it! They talk without words.
1.ko: Signs ask for the pitch in secret.

opts.a: To ask the pitcher for the pitch without talking

2.q: Where does the catcher hide the hand giving signs?
2.ko: If the other team sees it, they find out the plan.

opts.a: Between his legs, where the other team can't see it

3.q: If the pitcher doesn't understand the sign, he should pitch by guessing
3.ko: False: ask for time and talk.

4.q: In kids' leagues, who often decides which pitch to call?
4.ok: That's it! The coach helps.
4.ko: Coach → catcher → pitcher: that's how the sign travels.

opts.a: The coach, who passes the sign to the catcher

5.q: Tap the player who first gets the coach's sign
5.ko: The coach passes it to the catcher.

6.q: Signs are shown openly so everyone can see them
6.ko: False: they are hidden from the other team.

13.3.title: Blocking the ball in the dirt
13.3.objective: Learn the blocking technique: drop to your knees in front of the ball that bounces, with your body behind it, so it bounces close and no runner moves up for free.
demo: Sometimes the pitch hits the dirt and comes bouncing at you.
Don't try to catch it with one hand: block it!
Blocking is dropping to your knees right in front of the ball, with your chest leaning forward and the mitt covering the gap between your legs.
The ball hits your chest protector and drops dead in front of you, close by.
That way no runner moves up.
Blocking hurts a little sometimes, and that's why you wear your full armor.

1.q: What does the catcher do when the pitch hits the dirt?
1.ko: Your body is the wall: the ball drops in front of you.

opts.a: He blocks it, dropping to his knees in front of the ball
opts.b: He steps aside and lets it go by

2.q: Where should the blocked ball land?
2.ko: If it lands in front, you pick it up fast and nobody moves up.

opts.a: In front of the catcher, close by

3.q: To block, it's enough to reach one hand toward the bouncing ball
3.ok: Good! You block with your body.
3.ko: False: knees down and body behind the ball.

4.q: Which picture shows a good block?
4.ok: That's it! That's the way.
4.ko: Knees, chest and mitt covering the gap.

opts.a: Catcher on his knees, chest leaning and mitt between his legs

5.q: What is a good block for?
5.ko: Ball under control, runners stay put.

opts.a: So no runner moves up on a loose ball

6.q: Blocking is done without gear because the ball comes slowly
6.ko: False: you block with your full gear on.

13.4.title: Catcher's interference
13.4.objective: Understand catcher's interference: if his glove touches the bat on the swing, or gets in the batter's way, the batter gets first base.
demo: The catcher lives right next to the batter, and sometimes this happens: the batter swings and his bat brushes the catcher's mitt.
That's catcher's interference.
Nobody did it on purpose, but the rule protects the batter: if the glove got in the way of the swing, the batter goes to first base.
That's why the catcher sets up close, but not too close: he leaves just enough room to catch without touching the bat.

1.q: What is catcher's interference?
1.ko: If the glove gets in the way of the swing, there is interference.

opts.a: His glove touches the bat or gets in the way of the batter's swing
opts.b: The catcher talks with the pitcher

2.q: If there is catcher's interference, what does the batter get?
2.ko: The rule protects his swing: first base.

opts.a: First base

3.q: Catcher's interference is always on purpose
3.ko: False: it's usually an accidental brush.

4.q: How does the catcher avoid interference?
4.ok: That's it! Close, not on top.
4.ko: Just enough room: you catch without touching the bat.

opts.a: Setting up close, but leaving room for the bat

5.q: The bat brushes the mitt on the swing. What happens?
5.ko: A brush on the swing: the batter gets first.

opts.a: Catcher's interference: batter to first

6.q: If the glove touches the bat, the batter is out
6.ko: False: it's the other way around, the batter goes to first.

13.5.title: The play at the plate
13.5.objective: Defend home on a close play: catch the throw at the plate, tag the runner without blocking his path when you don't have the ball, and take care of both players' bodies.
demo: The runner is coming home and the throw is coming from the outfield!
The play at the plate is the most exciting one.
The catcher sets up next to the plate, catches the ball and tags the runner with it.
But careful: without the ball, you can't cover the plate or block the runner's path; ball first, then the tag.
And the runner can't crash into you on purpose either: both take care of each other.
Ball, tag, and wait for the umpire's call!

1.q: On the play at the plate, what does the catcher need first?
1.ko: Without the ball there is no tag that counts.

opts.a: To catch the ball, and then tag the runner
opts.b: To cover the plate without the ball

2.q: The catcher can block the plate without having the ball
2.ok: Good! That gets in the runner's way.
2.ko: False: without the ball, you don't block the path.

3.q: How is the out made at home?
3.ok: Correct! A tag with the ball.
3.ko: A clean tag, before the plate: out.

opts.a: Tagging the runner with the ball before he touches the plate

4.q: The runner can crash into the catcher on purpose
4.ok: Good! Nobody crashes on purpose.
4.ko: False: both players take care of each other.

5.q: Tap the plate the runner must touch to score
5.ko: That's where the run scores.

6.q: The catcher tags the runner with the ball before the plate. What does the umpire call?
6.ko: Tag before the plate: out.

opts.a: Out!

14.1.title: The ready position
14.1.objective: Take the ready position on every pitch: feet apart, knees bent, glove down and eyes on the batter, ready to move to either side.
demo: Before every pitch, the whole infield gets into the ready position.
Feet apart, knees a little bent, weight forward, glove down and eyes on the batter.
No standing straight looking at the clouds: the ball can come to you on any pitch.
When the pitcher pitches, take a short little step and be ready.
Ready isn't a pose: it's being awake with your whole body.

1.q: What does the ready position look like?
1.ko: That way you can take off to either side.

opts.a: Feet apart, knees bent and glove down

2.q: The ready position is only used with two outs
2.ko: False: you repeat it on every pitch.

3.q: Where do your eyes look in the ready position?
3.ko: The ball is the boss: always watch it.

opts.a: At the batter and the ball

4.q: Which picture shows a player who is ready?
4.ok: That's it! That one is ready.
4.ko: Glove down and body forward.

opts.a: Player leaning forward, glove down and feet apart
opts.b: Player with his back to the batter

5.q: When do you get into the ready position?
5.ko: Every pitch can come to you.

opts.a: On every pitch, before the ball comes out
opts.c: At the end of the game

6.q: Being ready means staying still like a statue
6.ok: Good! Ready means able to move.
6.ko: False: it's being ready to take off, not frozen.

14.2.title: Fielding a ground ball
14.2.objective: Field a ground ball step by step: get in front of the ball, open glove on the ground, the other hand on top, and watch the ball until it goes into the glove.
demo: A ground ball comes at you.
Don't wait for it sideways: get in front of it and field it.
Lower your open glove all the way to the ground, like a little shovel, and put your other hand gently on top so the ball doesn't get away.
Watch the ball until it goes into your glove: eyes on the ball, always.
Then, feet toward the base and a safe throw.
In front, glove down, two hands and eyes on the ball: that's the ground ball recipe.

1.q: How do you wait for a ground ball?
1.ko: Your body behind the ball stops it all.

opts.a: Facing the ball, with the glove on the ground

2.q: What does your free hand do when fielding?
2.ko: Glove and hand: the ball doesn't get away.

opts.a: It goes on top of the glove to secure the ball

3.q: When fielding, you close your eyes at the last moment
3.ko: False: watch it until it goes into the glove.

4.q: Put the ground ball steps in order: in front of the ball, glove on the ground, secure with two hands, throw to the base
4.ok: Perfect! That's the order.
4.ko: In front, down, two hands and throw.

5.q: Why does the glove go all the way down to the ground?
5.ko: Glove on the ground: the ball goes in or hits you, but doesn't get through.

opts.a: So the ball doesn't go underneath

6.q: A ground ball is fielded the same way standing up, without getting low
6.ok: Correct! You have to get low.
6.ko: False: knees bent and glove down.

14.3.title: Receiving at the base
14.3.objective: Receive the throw at the base: get there in time, step on the base as the play needs, give a clear target with the glove and secure the ball before looking for the next out.
demo: A good throw is useless if nobody receives it well.
Receiving a throw at the base means getting there in time, setting up next to the base and showing your open glove like a big target for your teammate.
Catch it, secure the ball with two hands, and only then look for the next throw.
First the out at your base; the double play comes after.
No rushing and without dropping the ball.

1.q: What should the player receiving at the base show?
1.ko: That way your teammate knows where to throw.

opts.a: The open glove, like a clear target

2.q: What do you secure first at the base?
2.ko: Ball secure and out first; the rest comes after.

opts.a: The out at your base, with the ball secure
opts.b: The next throw, any way possible

3.q: To save time, you have to let go of the ball fast even if it isn't secure in the glove
3.ko: False: if it isn't secure, there's no out.

4.q: Tap the base the first baseman steps on for the force out
4.ok: That's it! First base.
4.ko: Feet on the base and glove to the throw.

5.q: If the throw comes a little off, what does the receiver do?
5.ok: Correct! The ball is the boss.
5.ko: Catching it is worth more than staying on the base.

opts.a: He leaves the base to get the ball and then tags or goes back
opts.c: He lets the ball go by

6.q: The receiver must get to the base before his teammate's throw comes out
6.ko: True: getting there late leaves the base empty.

14.4.title: Who covers second on the double play?
14.4.objective: Know who goes to cover the base at second depending on which side the ground ball goes: if it goes to the shortstop, the second baseman covers; if it goes to the second baseman, the shortstop covers.
demo: Quick review: the double play makes two outs on one play.
Now look at the secret: who waits at second to receive the first throw?
It depends on where the ground ball goes.
If the ground ball goes to the shortstop, the one who covers second is the second baseman.
If it goes to the second baseman, the shortstop covers.
The one who fields doesn't cover his own base: the teammate on the other side covers.
Each one knows his job before the pitch, without yelling or doubting.

1.q: Ground ball to the shortstop. Who covers second?
1.ko: The shortstop fields; the second baseman receives at second.

opts.a: The second baseman

2.q: Ground ball to the second baseman. Who covers second?
2.ok: Correct! The other way around too.
2.ko: Whoever doesn't field, covers.

opts.a: The shortstop

3.q: The player who fields the ground ball must also run to cover second
3.ko: False: one fields and the other covers.

4.q: When is it decided who covers second?
4.ok: That's it! No improvising.
4.ko: The plan is known before the play.

opts.a: Before the pitch, each one knows his job

5.q: Tap the base where the first out of the double play is made
5.ko: Second base first, then the throw to first.

6.q: On the double play, the throw to first goes before the one to second
6.ko: False: second for the first out, first for the second out.

14.5.title: Mine! Calling for the fly ball
14.5.objective: Call for the ball out loud on a fly ball ("Mine!", "I got it!") when you are going to catch it, and get out of the way and back up when a teammate calls it, so nobody crashes.
demo: A fly ball goes up and two teammates run toward the ball.
If nobody talks, they crash and the ball drops.
The solution is to yell "Mine!" or "I got it!"
If you're going to catch it, you yell it loud and early, and the ball is yours.
If your teammate yells it, you answer, get out of the way and back him up in case it gets away from him.
One ball, one voice.
Talking on defense isn't noise: it's safety.

1.q: What do you yell when you're going to catch a fly ball?
1.ko: Your call warns the whole team.

opts.a: "Mine!" or "I got it!"

2.q: Your teammate yells "Mine!". What do you do?
2.ok: Correct! One catches, the other backs up.
2.ko: No crashes and with backup.

opts.a: You get out of the way and back him up
opts.b: You keep running and crash into him

3.q: Calling for the ball is only so the crowd knows who catches it
3.ok: Good! It's so you don't crash.
3.ko: False: it's safety between teammates.

4.q: When do you have to yell "Mine!"?
4.ok: That's it! Early.
4.ko: If you yell late, your teammate is already right there.

opts.a: Loud and early, as soon as you decide to go for the ball
opts.b: At the end, when you already have it

5.q: If two players yell "Mine!" at the same time, both should keep running
5.ko: False: one gets out of the way; in Level 15 you'll see who has priority.

6.q: Which picture shows good communication?
6.ko: One voice, one catch, zero crashes.

opts.a: One player yells "Mine!" and the other gets out of the way

15.1.title: The first step: backwards
15.1.objective: Understand that on a high or deep hit, the outfielder's first step goes back, so he doesn't come up short; the ball that drops in front can be reached running, the one that goes over his head can't.
demo: In the outfield there's a golden rule: your first step goes back.
When the ball goes up high and far, if you take a step forward and the ball goes over your head, you never catch up to it.
But if your first step goes back and the ball drops in front of you, you can run in and get to it.
Back first, and then you adjust.
It's better to run forward than to watch the ball drop behind you.

1.q: Where does the outfielder's first step go on a high hit?
1.ko: The one that drops in front can be reached; the one that goes over can't.

opts.a: Backwards

2.q: If the outfielder takes his first step forward and the ball goes over his head, he can still reach it running backwards
2.ok: Good! He almost never catches up to it.
2.ko: False: that's why the first step goes back.

3.q: Which ball can you reach?
3.ko: You run forward and go get it.

opts.a: The one that drops in front of you
opts.b: The one that already left the field
opts.c: The one that went way over your head

4.q: Which picture shows the good first step?
4.ok: That's it! That one gets there.
4.ko: First back, then to the ball.

opts.a: Outfielder turning back as the ball is hit
opts.b: Outfielder coming in toward the infield

5.q: When do you decide your first step?
5.ko: Reading fast is half the catch.

opts.a: As soon as the ball is hit, reading how high it goes
opts.b: When the ball has already landed

6.q: The first step back also works for balls that drop short
6.ko: True: back first and you adjust running forward.

15.2.title: Whose fly ball is it? The center's priority
15.2.objective: Understand priority in the outfield: the center fielder is in charge of the middle; if he calls for the ball, the corner outfielders give way and back up.
demo: In Level 14 you learned to yell "Mine!"; this is review.
Now, who wins when two outfielders can get there?
The center fielder is in charge: he sees the whole field in front of him and covers the middle.
If the center fielder calls for the ball, the left and right fielders give way, step aside and back up.
It's called priority.
Only one voice is in charge in the middle, and it's the center fielder's.

1.q: Who is in charge of the fly balls in the middle of the outfield?
1.ok: That's it! The center is in charge.
1.ko: He sees everything in front of him: his word rules.

opts.a: The center fielder
opts.c: The tallest player on the team

2.q: The center fielder yells "Mine!". What does the left fielder do?
2.ok: Correct! Give way and back up.
2.ko: No crashes and with backup, as always.

opts.a: He gives way, steps aside and backs up
opts.b: He keeps running the same way

3.q: The center fielder's priority means he catches every ball in the outfield
3.ok: Good! He only rules the doubtful ones.
3.ko: False: each one catches his own; the center decides the ones in the middle.

4.q: Why is the center fielder in charge?
4.ok: That's it! His view is in charge.
4.ko: From in front you read the ball better.

opts.a: Because he sees the whole field in front of him and covers the middle

5.q: Tap the position of the outfielder who is in charge of the middle
5.ko: Center of the outfield: the general out there.

6.q: If nobody calls a ball between two outfielders, it's safer to let it drop
6.ok: Correct! Someone has to call it.
6.ko: False: with no voice there's a crash or a dropped ball.

15.3.title: A real catch or a trap
15.3.objective: Tell apart the legal catch (the ball stays secure in the glove or hand without touching the ground) from the trap (the ball touches the ground before or at the same time), which isn't a catch and doesn't make an out.
demo: The outfielder dives, the ball goes into the glove… but first it brushed the grass.
Out or not?
Here's the difference: a catch is when the ball stays secure in your glove or your hand without having touched the ground.
If the ball touches the ground before or at the same time, even if it ends up in your glove afterward, it's a trap, and it's not a catch: the batter isn't out on that play.
The umpire looks at just one thing: did it touch the ground or not?

1.q: What is a real catch?
1.ok: That's it! Without touching the ground.
1.ko: Secure and without bouncing: a catch.

opts.a: The ball stays secure in the glove or hand without touching the ground
opts.b: The ball bounces and then goes into the glove
opts.c: The ball ends up under your body

2.q: The ball brushed the grass and then stayed in the glove. What is it?
2.ko: It touched the ground: it doesn't count as a catch.

opts.a: A trap: it's not a catch

3.q: With a trap, the batter is out anyway because the ball ended up in the glove
3.ok: Good! A trap isn't an out.
3.ko: False: the ball is still in play and you have to play it.

4.q: If there is a trap, what should the outfielder do?
4.ok: That's it! The play goes on.
4.ko: No celebrating: live ball, throw it.

opts.a: Pick up the ball and throw fast to a base
opts.c: Show the glove to the crowd

5.q: A ball that bounces before going into the outfielder's glove. What does the umpire decide?
5.ko: It bounced first: the game goes on.

opts.a: It's not a catch: ball in play

6.q: For it to be a catch, the ball can bounce once on the ground if the glove covers it
6.ko: False: one touch of the ground and it's already a trap.

15.4.title: Keeping the ball in front and the warning track
15.4.objective: Play the ball so it always stays in front of the outfielder, and know the warning track: the strip next to the fence that lets your feet know the wall is close.
demo: Two secrets of the outfield.
First: keep the ball in front.
If a hit bounces in front of you, pick it up calmly; if it gets past you on the side or over your head, the runners run and run.
That's why, when in doubt, you play a step farther back.
Second: next to the fence there's a strip of different dirt, the warning track.
When your feet feel it, the fence is very close: catch carefully and don't crash into the wall.

1.q: Why does the outfielder play a step farther back when in doubt?
1.ok: That's it! Ball in front, play alive.
1.ko: The ball that gets past you is worth many bases.

opts.a: So the ball always stays in front of him
opts.b: To be close to the dugout

2.q: What is the warning track?
2.ko: Different dirt underfoot: the fence is close.

opts.a: The strip next to the fence that warns you the wall is close

3.q: The warning track is in the middle of the outfield
3.ok: Good! It's next to the fence.
3.ko: False: it runs along the whole outfield, right by the wall.

4.q: How do you notice the warning track without looking down?
4.ok: That's it! You feel it with your feet.
4.ko: That way you watch the ball and not the ground.

opts.a: Your feet feel ground different from the grass

5.q: When you feel the warning track, you should run harder toward the fence
5.ok: Correct! It's a warning to be careful.
5.ko: False: it warns you so you don't crash.

6.q: Tap the strip of dirt that warns you you're about to hit the fence
6.ko: Right by the fence, all around the outfield.
6.answer: The warning track, next to the fence

15.5.title: Playing with the sun in your face
15.5.objective: Catch fly balls with the sun in your face: use the glove as a visor without covering the ball, turn a little sideways when you can, and ask for help out loud if you lose the ball.
demo: Some fly balls are tricky: the ones that come with the sun in your face.
The outfielders' trick: raise your glove and use it as a visor, to block the sun without blocking the ball; you watch the ball just past the side of the glove.
If you can, stand a little sideways so the sun doesn't hit you straight on.
And if you lose the ball in the glare, say it out loud: your teammate can back you up.
Losing it in silence is the only real mistake.

1.q: What do you use as a visor against the sun?
1.ok: That's it! Glove as a visor.
1.ko: You block the sun and see the ball from the side.

opts.a: The glove, blocking the sun without blocking the ball
opts.b: Only your free hand over your eyes

2.q: If you lose the ball in the sun, the best thing is to stay quiet
2.ok: Good! You have to say it.
2.ko: False: call it out loud and your teammate backs you up.

3.q: What else helps with the sun in your face?
3.ko: And your cap helps a little too.

opts.a: Standing a little sideways so it doesn't hit you straight on

4.q: Which picture shows the right technique?
4.ok: That's it! That's the way.
4.ko: Sun blocked, ball in sight.

opts.a: Outfielder with the glove raised like a visor watching the ball
opts.b: Outfielder covering his face with both hands
opts.c: Outfielder with his back to the hit

5.q: With the sun in his face, the outfielder should catch the same way without changing anything
5.ok: Correct! There's a technique for that.
5.ko: False: visor, sideways and voice: three helps.

6.q: Your teammate lost the ball in the sun and said so. What do you do?
6.ko: Warn and back up: that's how plays are saved.

opts.a: You run to back up the play

16.1.title: The batter's box, the stance and the grip
16.1.objective: Set up in the batter's box with your feet inside, a comfortable and balanced stance, and grip the bat firmly without squeezing it as if it were going to break.
demo: Your turn starts in the batter's box: that painted rectangle next to home.
Both feet go inside the box, apart, knees soft and weight balanced.
Your hands hold the bat firmly, but without squeezing it as if it were going to break: stiff hands, slow swing.
The bat rests on your back shoulder, ready.
Box, stance and grip.
From there, it's all about watching the ball.

1.q: Where do the batter's feet go?
1.ko: The box marks your place to bat.

opts.a: Inside the batter's box

2.q: How do you grip the bat?
2.ok: Correct! Firm and loose at the same time.
2.ko: Stiff hands make a slow swing.

opts.a: Firmly, without squeezing it as if it were going to break

3.q: The stance is feet together and a stiff body
3.ko: False: balance and soft knees.

4.q: Which picture shows a good stance?
4.ok: That's it! Ready to watch the ball.
4.ko: Box, feet and bat: everything in its place.

opts.a: Batter in the box, feet apart and bat on the back shoulder

5.q: What is a good stance for?
5.ko: Without balance, the swing falls apart.

opts.a: To be balanced and make a quick swing
opts.b: To look good in the photo

6.q: The batter can stand with one foot outside the box if it's comfortable for him
6.ko: False: both feet go inside the box.

16.2.title: Eyes on the ball from the pitcher's hand
16.2.objective: Watch the ball from the moment it leaves the pitcher's hand and follow it all the way to the bat, without looking away; and know the checked swing: starting the swing and stopping it, where the umpire decides if there was a swing.
demo: The secret of good hitters fits in one phrase: eyes on the ball from the pitcher's hand.
Look at his hand, find the ball when it comes out and follow it all the way to your bat.
And here's a curious play: sometimes you start to swing and stop halfway.
That's a checked swing: the motion started and stopped.
The home plate umpire decides: if he thinks the bat went through looking for the ball, he calls a strike; if you stopped in time, it's a ball.
Watching well also means knowing how to stop.

1.q: From when do you watch the ball?
1.ko: Following it all the way is the secret.

opts.a: From when it leaves the pitcher's hand

2.q: What is a checked swing?
2.ko: It started and stopped: a checked swing.

opts.a: Starting the swing and stopping it halfway

3.q: Who decides if the checked swing was a swing?
3.ko: If the bat went through looking for the ball, it's a strike.

opts.a: The home plate umpire

4.q: On a checked swing, the batter never moved the bat
4.ok: Good! He moved it, then stopped.
4.ko: False: the motion started and stopped.

5.q: Watching the pitcher's hand helps you see the ball earlier
5.ok: Correct! You see it from the moment it's born.
5.ko: True: ball seen early, swing on time.

6.q: The batter started to swing and stopped without going after the ball. What can the umpire call?
6.ko: He stopped in time: ball.

opts.a: Ball! There was no swing

16.3.title: The foul tip: the speedy brush
16.3.objective: Understand the foul tip: the ball that brushes the bat and the catcher catches directly is a strike and the ball stays live; if he doesn't catch it, it's a regular foul.
demo: Listen to the faintest sound in baseball: tick!
The ball barely brushes the bat, shoots back and the catcher catches it directly, without it touching the ground.
That's a foul tip.
It's not a regular foul: if the catcher catches it, it counts as a strike and the ball stays live, like any other pitch.
It can even be the third strike and a strikeout.
But if the catcher doesn't catch it and the ball drops, then it's a regular foul and the ball stops.
Brush, catch and strike: foul tip.

1.q: What is a foul tip?
1.ko: Brush and a direct catch by the catcher.

opts.a: The ball brushes the bat and the catcher catches it directly
opts.b: A very high foul to the outfield
opts.c: A bad pitch by the pitcher

2.q: A caught foul tip counts as a strike
2.ok: Good! A strike, not a free foul.
2.ko: True: caught, the brush counts as a strike.

3.q: If the catcher doesn't catch the brush and the ball drops, what is it?
3.ko: The direct catch is what changes everything.

opts.a: A regular foul and the ball stops

4.q: With a caught foul tip, does the ball stay live?
4.ok: That's it! Live ball.
4.ko: That's why runners have to be careful.

opts.a: Yes, it stays live like any other pitch

5.q: A brush off the bat, a direct catch by the catcher with two strikes. What does the umpire call?
5.ok: Good! Strikeout on a foul tip.
5.ko: Caught with two strikes: the third strike.

opts.a: Strike three! Out!

6.q: Every brush off the bat is a foul tip even if the catcher doesn't catch the ball
6.ok: Correct! No catch, no foul tip.
6.ko: False: without a direct catch, it's a regular foul.

16.4.title: The sacrifice bunt and the lane to first
16.4.objective: Use the bunt as a sacrifice (review of the bunt): move a teammate up while accepting your own out; and run to first in the runner's lane without getting in the way of the throw.
demo: Applied review: you already know the bunt.
Today you use it for a big purpose: the sacrifice bunt.
Your teammate is on base and you bunt softly so he moves up, even if you're put out at first.
You sacrifice yourself for the team, and that's why it has that name.
And when you run to first, stay in your path: the runner's lane, marked next to the line.
The last part of the way is run inside the lane, in foul territory: if you run inside the field and get in the way of the throw to first, the umpire can call you out for interference.
Bunt, move your teammate up and run in your lane.

1.q: What is the sacrifice bunt for?
1.ko: You sacrifice yourself: he moves up, you're out.

opts.a: For the teammate to move up a base, even if the batter is put out

2.q: What is the runner's lane?
2.ko: The last part is run inside it.

opts.a: The little path marked next to the line on the way to first

3.q: On a sacrifice bunt, the batter tries to be safe no matter what
3.ok: Good! He tries to move his teammate up.
3.ko: False: he accepts his out for the team.

4.q: What can happen if you run inside the field and get in the way of the throw to first?
4.ok: That's it! That's why the lane exists.
4.ko: Inside the lane, the throw goes by freely.

opts.a: The umpire can call you out for interference

5.q: Tap the lane the batter runs in to first
5.ko: Right by the line, on the foul side.
5.answer: The lane next to the first base line, in foul territory

6.q: The sacrifice bunt only works if the batter is also safe
6.ok: Correct! It works if the teammate moves up.
6.ko: False: his job is to move the runner.

16.5.title: Dropping the bat and wearing the helmet
16.5.objective: Let go of the bat without throwing it — drop it next to home — and run with your helmet on and fitted well, which stays on until you reach the dugout.
demo: You hit the ball.
And now?
Don't throw the bat: drop it softly next to home plate.
A flying bat can hit the catcher or the umpire.
And run with your helmet on: the helmet protects you from a wild throw or a fall, and it doesn't come off until you reach the dugout.
Smart hitters: bat on the ground, helmet on your head and run in the lane you already know.

1.q: What do you do with the bat after making contact?
1.ok: That's it! Bat on the ground.
1.ko: A flying bat can hit someone.

opts.a: You drop it softly next to home
opts.c: You carry it running to first

2.q: You can take your helmet off running to first if it gets in the way
2.ok: Good! Helmet on until the dugout.
2.ko: False: it protects you from throws and falls the whole way.

3.q: What does the helmet protect you from when running the bases?
3.ko: Wild throws happen: helmet on.

opts.a: From a wild throw or a fall

4.q: Who is near home and could get hit by a thrown bat?
4.ok: That's it! They're right there.
4.ko: Because of them you drop it, you don't throw it.

opts.a: The catcher and the umpire

5.q: A well-fitted helmet doesn't move even if you run fast
5.ko: True: if it wobbles on your head, ask for help to fit it.

6.q: Which picture shows the right batter after making contact?
6.ok: That's it! That's how it's done.
6.ko: Bat down, helmet up, run.

opts.a: Bat dropping next to home and runner with his helmet on

17.1.title: The intentional walk
17.1.objective: Understand that the defense sometimes decides not to compete against a dangerous batter and sends him to first on purpose, and that the way it's given changes by league: ask the coach.
demo: The other team's strongest batter is up and first base is open.
Sometimes the defense makes a cool-headed decision: not compete with him and send him to first, walking, on purpose.
That's the intentional walk.
It's not fear: it's strategy, to look for an easier out against the next batter.
Careful: the way it's given changes by league — in some the balls are pitched, in others it's enough to tell the umpire.
It may be different in your league: ask your coach how it's done.

1.q: What is the intentional walk?
1.ko: Strategy, not an accident.

opts.a: Sending the batter to first on purpose, without competing with him

2.q: Why is an intentional walk given?
2.ok: Correct! You think as a team.
2.ko: You trade a dangerous batter for an easier one.

opts.a: To look for an easier out against the next batter

3.q: The intentional walk means the team is afraid and plays badly
3.ko: False: the best teams use it, thinking.

4.q: How is the intentional walk given in your league?
4.ok: That's it! Each league has its way.
4.ko: It may be different in your league: ask your coach.

opts.a: However my league says: ask your coach

5.q: With first base occupied, giving the intentional walk is usually a bad idea
5.ok: Correct! You load the bases for free.
5.ko: True: it's mostly used with first base open.

6.q: The defense announces it is sending the batter to first on purpose. What happens?
6.ko: Decision announced: to first.

opts.a: Intentional walk: the batter goes to first
opts.c: Dead ball and nobody moves up

17.2.title: The hit and run
17.2.objective: Understand the hit and run: the runner takes off with the pitch and the batter looks for contact to put the ball in play and protect him.
demo: The coach crosses his arms and calls a brave play: the hit and run.

It works like this: the runner on first takes off with the pitch, as if he were stealing, and the batter swings looking for contact, even if the pitch isn't perfect, to put the ball in play and protect the runner.
If the ball goes through the hole left by the fielder who covered second, it's perfect!
It's a job for two: one runs, the other protects.

1.q: What is the hit and run?
1.ok: That's it! A play for two.
1.ko: One runs and the other protects him by hitting.

opts.a: The runner takes off with the pitch and the batter looks for contact

2.q: Why does the batter look for contact even if the pitch is bad?
2.ko: Without contact, the runner is left hanging on the steal.

opts.a: To protect the runner who already took off

3.q: On the hit and run, the runner waits on his base to see the hit
3.ok: Good! He takes off with the pitch.
3.ko: False: he takes off with the pitch, without waiting.

4.q: What hole does the ball use on the hit and run?
4.ok: That's it! That's where the ball goes through.
4.ko: The defense moves and the hole appears.

opts.a: The one left by the fielder who went to cover second
opts.c: None, you always hit it in the air

5.q: The hit and run is a play the coach calls with a sign
5.ko: True: that's why you have to watch the signs.

6.q: If the batter doesn't hit the ball on the hit and run, what's waiting for the runner?
6.ko: With no hit, the runner is alone against the throw.

opts.a: A possible out stealing, because he left without protection
opts.b: Nothing, he goes back for free

17.3.title: The squeeze: the bunt that scores
17.3.objective: Understand the squeeze: with a runner on third, the batter bunts so the runner scores; on the suicide squeeze the runner takes off with the pitch.
demo: The boldest play with a runner on third: the squeeze play.
The batter bunts the ball very softly and the runner on third runs home to score.
There's an even braver version: the suicide squeeze, where the runner takes off with the pitch, before knowing if the bunt worked.
If the batter misses the bunt, the runner is caught without a base.
That's why the squeeze is practiced a lot and only called when the coach trusts the bunt.

1.q: What is the squeeze for?
1.ko: The soft ball brings the run home.

opts.a: For the runner on third to score on a bunt

2.q: What does the batter do on the squeeze?
2.ko: His only job: the ball has to touch the bat.

opts.a: He bunts the ball softly to move it away from home
opts.c: He steps away from the pitch

3.q: On the suicide squeeze, the runner waits at third until he sees the bunt
3.ok: Good! He takes off with the pitch.
3.ko: False: that's why it's so bold, he leaves early.

4.q: If the batter misses the bunt on the suicide squeeze, what happens to the runner?
4.ok: That's it! That's the risk.
4.ko: No bunt, and the runner is left hanging.

opts.a: He's caught on the way home, almost defenseless
opts.c: He goes back to third with no problem

5.q: The squeeze is only called when the coach trusts the batter's bunt
5.ko: True: it's a play of practice, not luck.

6.q: Tap the base the squeeze runner starts from
6.ko: Third to home: that's the squeeze.

17.4.title: The defense adjusts
17.4.objective: Understand defensive positioning: the defense adjusts to the batter and the situation: infield in to go for the out at home, infield back for the double play, and outfielders according to the batter's strength.
demo: The defense doesn't always stand the same way: it adjusts its positioning.
If there's a runner on third and the game is close, the infield plays in, right at the edge of the grass, to throw home fast.
If you're looking for the double play, the infield plays back, calmly, in its usual spot.
With a very strong batter, the outfielders take steps back.
Each position tells a story: the coach reads the game and moves his players like chess pieces.

1.q: Why does the defense change position depending on the play?
1.ok: That's it! Each spot has a plan.
1.ko: Position is strategy.

opts.a: To get ready for the play that suits it best
opts.c: Because it gets bored in the same spot

2.q: Runner on third and a close game, how does the infield play?
2.ko: Close to home to defend the run.

opts.a: In, close, to throw home fast
opts.b: Way back, next to the outfield

3.q: When does the infield play back, in its normal spot?
3.ok: Good! Back for the double play.
3.ko: Far from home, the throw home would be late: better two outs.

opts.a: When it's calmly looking for the double play
opts.b: When there's a runner on third and a close game

4.q: Against a very strong batter, the outfielders usually take steps back
4.ok: Correct! They respect his strength.
4.ko: True: room behind for the deep balls.

5.q: Who decides how the defense adjusts?
5.ok: That's it! He reads and moves.
5.ko: He moves his players like chess pieces.

opts.a: The coach, reading the game

6.q: Adjusting the defense is cheating
6.ko: False: each team sets up however suits it best.

17.5.title: The score decides the play and the walk-off
17.5.objective: Read the score, inning and outs before every play to decide risks; and know the walk-off: the hit that wins the game in the last chance and ends it that very instant.
demo: Before every play, Hall of Fame players look at three things: the score, the inning and the outs.
With the game tied at the end, a runner plays it differently than when winning by a lot.

And listen to what the happiest moment in baseball is called: if the home team bats in its last chance, tied or losing by a little, and a hit brings in the winning run, that's a walk-off: the game ends that very instant and everyone runs out to celebrate, because the other team has no more turns.
If the home team is already winning when that turn comes, it doesn't even need to be played: the game is already over.
The score isn't just numbers: it decides which risk is worth taking.

1.q: What three things do you look at before every play?
1.ok: That's it! Three facts, one decision.
1.ko: With them you know which risk is worth it.

opts.a: Score, inning and outs
opts.b: The crowd, the weather and the dugout
opts.c: My average, my glove and my cap

2.q: What is a walk-off?
2.ko: Winning run and celebrate: there's no other turn.

opts.a: The home team's hit that wins the game in its last chance and ends it instantly

3.q: Only the home team can get a walk-off, in its last chance at bat
3.ok: Good! That's how the play works.
3.ko: True: the visitor always leaves a turn to answer.

4.q: If the home team is already winning when its last turn comes, what happens?
4.ok: That's it! They already won.
4.ko: There's nothing to come back from: game over.

opts.a: The game is already over, it doesn't need to bat
opts.b: It bats anyway out of habit
opts.c: A turn is given to the other team

5.q: With the game wide open in your favor, it's best to take risks the same as in a tied game
5.ok: Correct! The score sets the risk.
5.ko: False: each score calls for its own play.

6.q: Home team's last chance, tied game, and a hit brings in the winning run. What happened?
6.ko: Winning run on the last turn: it's over.

opts.a: Walk-off! Game over
opts.b: The game goes on one more turn

18.1.title: Sliding safely
18.1.objective: Slide feet first, with your hands up and never into the fielder; and know that sliding head first may be banned in your league: ask the coach.
demo: You're running into the base and the throw is close: time to slide!
To slide is to drop down onto the ground to get in under the tag.
The safe way in kids' leagues is feet first: your legs go in front, your body leans back a little and your hands go up so you don't put them on the ground.
You never throw yourself into the fielder to knock him down: you go to the base, not to the player.
And careful: in many kids' leagues sliding head first is banned, because your head goes in front, unprotected.
It may be different in your league: ask your coach before you do it.

1.q: What's the safe way to slide in kids' leagues?
1.ko: Legs in front and hands up: safe.

opts.a: Feet first, with your hands up
opts.b: Head first, with your hands in front

2.q: When you slide, you have to put your hands on the ground to brake
2.ko: False: putting your hands down can hurt your wrists.

3.q: What does a runner slide into?
3.ko: The fielder isn't something to crash into.

opts.a: Into the base, never into the fielder
opts.b: Into the fielder to knock him down

4.q: Can you slide head first in your league?
4.ok: That's it! Ask first.
4.ko: It may be different in your league: ask your coach.

opts.a: It depends on my league: ask your coach

5.q: Sliding helps you get in under the fielder's tag
5.ko: True: low and fast to the base.

6.q: Which picture shows the safe slide?
6.ok: That's it! That one arrives safely.
6.ko: Feet first, always in kids' leagues.

opts.a: Runner feet first with hands up

18.2.title: The mercy rule
18.2.objective: Understand the mercy rule: if one team is winning by a very big difference, the game can end early to look after the kids; each league sets the exact difference.
demo: Imagine a game where one team scores and scores and the other can't climb out of the hole.
Going on like that doesn't teach anything anymore, it only tires and saddens.
That's what the mercy rule is for: if the run difference goes past the limit the league sets, the game ends early, with respect for both teams.
What that difference is and from when it counts is set by each league, and it changes with age.
Here you don't learn a number: you learn the idea.
It may be different in your league: ask your coach what the limit is.

1.q: What is the mercy rule for?
1.ok: That's it! It looks after everyone.
1.ko: Winning with respect is baseball too.

opts.a: To end a game with a huge difference early, looking after the kids

2.q: Who sets the run difference for the mercy rule?
2.ko: It may be different in your league: ask your coach.

opts.a: Each league, depending on age

3.q: The mercy rule has the same number of runs in every league
3.ok: Good! It changes by league and age.
3.ko: False: that's why you don't learn a fixed number.

4.q: When the mercy rule is applied, the team that is winning wins the game
4.ok: Correct! The result stands.
4.ko: True: the game ends with that score.

5.q: What should the team that is winning by a lot do?
5.ko: Today's opponent is a baseball teammate too.

opts.a: Play with respect, never making fun of the other team

6.q: The difference went past the league's limit. What does the umpire decide?
6.ko: Their league's limit is what counts.

opts.a: Game over by that league's mercy rule

18.3.title: Official game, suspended game and extra innings
18.3.objective: Understand that a game becomes official once what the league requires has been played; that if the weather stops it, it can be suspended and continue another day; and that if the official game ends tied, some leagues play extra innings until someone wins.
demo: Three big-game words.
Official game: once the part the league requires has been played, the result counts even if something happens afterward.

If lightning strikes or it gets dark and the game has to stop — safety review: with lightning you leave the field — the game can be suspended and finished another day from where it stopped, if the league says so.
And if an official game ends tied, some leagues keep going with extra innings: new turns, one for each team, until one ends up ahead.
How much it takes for a game to be official and whether there are extra innings is set by each league: ask your coach.

1.q: What is an official game?
1.ok: That's it! A result that counts.
1.ko: What your league requires, not a number from this game.

opts.a: One that has already played what the league requires for the result to count
opts.c: The first game of the year

2.q: What is a suspended game?
2.ko: Bad weather today, ending another day.

opts.a: A stopped game that can be finished another day from where it stopped

3.q: With lightning nearby, the game goes on until the inning ends
3.ko: False: lightning means leaving the field without waiting.

4.q: What are extra innings?
4.ok: That's it! To break the tie.
4.ko: One for each team, until someone ends up ahead.

opts.a: New turns to break the tie in a tied official game

5.q: Do all leagues have extra innings?
5.ko: It may be different in your league: ask your coach.

opts.a: No: each league sets it, ask your coach
opts.b: Yes, the same in all of them

6.q: If a suspended game continues another day, it starts from zero
6.ok: Good! It continues where it stopped.
6.ko: False: it picks up from the point where it stopped, if the league says so.

18.4.title: Substitutions, re-entry and batting out of order
18.4.objective: Understand substitution (the player who comes in takes the batting spot of the one who left), that whether the player who left can come back (re-entry) is set by the league, and that batting out of order is a mistake the defense can point out to the umpire.
demo: A game also moves from the dugout.
When a new player comes in, it's a substitution: the one who comes in takes over the spot in the batting order of the one who left, and the coach tells the umpire.
Can the one who left come back?
That's called re-entry, and each league sets it: in some yes and in others no; ask your coach.
And watch out for this mistake: if someone bats in another player's turn, that's batting out of order.
If the defense notices and tells the umpire in time, there's a penalty; that's why the coach and the captain guard the lineup card like a treasure.

1.q: When a substitute comes in, which batting spot does he take?
1.ok: That's it! He takes over the turn.
1.ko: He comes in for someone and takes his spot.

opts.a: That of the player who left

2.q: Can the player who left come back into the game?
2.ko: It may be different in your league: ask your coach.

opts.a: It depends on my league's re-entry: ask your coach

3.q: What is batting out of order?
3.ko: The card sets the order of the turns.

opts.a: Batting in another player's turn
opts.c: Batting lefty when you are a righty

4.q: If nobody notices the batting out of order in time, the game can go on
4.ok: Good! The appeal has its moment.
4.ko: True: that's why the defense watches the card too.

5.q: Who tells the umpire about a change?
5.ko: A change without telling doesn't count.

opts.a: The coach

6.q: The captain can help by making sure the batting order is respected
6.ko: True: guarding the card is teamwork.

18.5.title: The courtesy runner
18.5.objective: Understand the special or courtesy runner that some leagues allow for the catcher (and sometimes the pitcher), so he can get ready without stopping the game; it only exists if the league allows it.
demo: The catcher works hard: every inning he has to put on all his armor.

Some leagues give him a hand with the courtesy runner: if the catcher gets on base when there are already two outs, a teammate from the dugout can run for him, so the catcher can go get dressed and the next inning doesn't stop.
Some leagues also allow it for the pitcher.
But careful: this doesn't exist in every league, or with the same rules.
It's an extra some leagues allow, not a rule for everyone.
It may be different in your league: ask your coach if it exists and how it works.

1.q: What is a courtesy runner?
1.ok: That's it! Help for the catcher.
1.ko: He runs for him while he puts on his armor.

opts.a: A teammate who runs for the catcher so he can get ready
opts.b: The fastest runner in the world
opts.c: A runner from the other team

2.q: Why is it used with the catcher?
2.ko: Armor on in time, inning with no wait.

opts.a: Because putting on the armor takes time and the game doesn't stop
opts.b: So the catcher rests the whole game

3.q: The courtesy runner exists the same way in every league
3.ko: False: it may be different in your league: ask your coach.

4.q: When does the runner for the catcher usually come in?
4.ok: That's it! With two outs.
4.ko: That way he gets dressed while the inning ends.

opts.a: When the catcher is on base with two outs
opts.b: At any moment of the game

5.q: Some leagues also allow a courtesy runner for the pitcher
5.ko: True: depending on the league, the pitcher too.

6.q: If your league doesn't have a courtesy runner, what does the catcher on base do?
6.ko: Without that rule, everyone runs his own base.

opts.a: He runs himself like any player

19.1.title: Warming up before playing
19.1.objective: Warm up before every game and practice: move your body little by little, loosen your arms without throwing hard at first, and never throw all-out with a cold body.
demo: No player goes onto the field cold.
To warm up is to wake up your body little by little: first move and jog gently, then stretch and move your arms, and throw starting short and soft, moving farther apart little by little.
Throwing hard with a cold body is asking your arm for trouble.
And you already know this, as a review: if something hurts while you warm up, you stop and tell an adult.
Warming up isn't wasting time: it's the first play of the day.

1.q: What is warming up before playing for?
1.ok: That's it! A body awake is a body looked after.
1.ko: Warming up is the first play of the day.

opts.a: To wake up the body little by little and look after the muscles and the arm
opts.b: To get tired before the game
opts.c: So the coach doesn't scold you

2.q: How do the warm-up throws start?
2.ko: A cold arm isn't pushed to the max.

opts.a: Short and soft, moving farther apart little by little

3.q: If something hurts while warming up, you keep going the same so you don't lose your turn (review)
3.ok: Good! Pain means stop and tell (review).
3.ko: False: you stop and tell an adult.

4.q: What comes first in the warm-up?
4.ok: That's it! First, move.
4.ko: Little by little: that's the order.

opts.a: Moving and jogging gently

5.q: Warming up is a waste of time because it doesn't count as playing
5.ok: Correct! It's part of the game.
5.ko: False: without warming up, the body arrives asleep and gets hurt.

6.q: Tap the player who is warming up the right way
6.ok: Good! That one looks after his arm.
6.ko: Soft and close first: that's how you warm up.

opts.a: The one throwing soft and close, building up little by little
opts.b: The one throwing all-out from the first throw

19.2.title: Water, shade and rest
19.2.objective: Look after yourself in the heat: drink water (hydration) before, during and after, find the shade in the dugout and rest; and if a kid feels bad, dizzy or in pain, he stops and tells an adult right away.
demo: The sun plays too, and sometimes it plays hard.
Your plan against the heat has three parts: water, shade and rest.
Drink water before playing, between innings and when you finish, without waiting until you are very thirsty.
In the dugout, find the shade.
And listen to your body: if you feel dizzy, have a headache, feel sick to your stomach or strange, you stop right away and tell an adult.
No toughing it out like a hero: telling early is what smart players do.
That's what the coach and parents are there for.

1.q: What are the three helpers against the heat?
1.ko: Water always, shade in the dugout and breaks.

opts.a: Water, shade and rest

2.q: You have to wait until you are extremely thirsty to drink water
2.ok: Good! You drink before and often.
2.ko: False: water goes before, during and after.

3.q: You feel dizzy and strange during the game. What do you do?
3.ko: Dizzy or unwell: stop and tell, always.

opts.a: I stop and tell an adult right away
opts.b: I keep playing without saying anything

4.q: Where do you sit in the dugout on a sunny day?
4.ok: That's it! Shade that looks after you.
4.ko: The dugout is part of the plan too.

opts.a: In the shade, resting

5.q: Putting up with feeling unwell without saying anything is what brave players do
5.ko: False: telling early protects your health.

6.q: Which picture shows the right care on a hot day?
6.ok: That's it! That one looks after himself.
6.ko: Water and shade: the full plan.

opts.a: Kid drinking water in the shade in the dugout
opts.b: Kid playing with no water under strong sun

19.3.title: Breathing through the nerves
19.3.objective: Know a short routine for nerves: breathe slowly, look at a fixed point, tell yourself a short phrase ("I can handle this at-bat") and think only about the next play.
demo: Is your heart beating fast before you bat?
Congratulations: those are nerves, and they happen to everyone, even the pros.

Your short routine has four steps: breathe slowly, letting the air out gently; look at a fixed point, like the ball or your base; tell yourself a short phrase, like "I can handle this at-bat"; and think only about the next play, not the whole game.
It's called a reset: starting over on the inside.
Nerves with a routine turn into energy.

1.q: What is the first step of the routine against nerves?
1.ko: Slow air calms the body.

opts.a: Breathing slowly, letting the air out gently

2.q: Which short phrase helps before your at-bat?
2.ok: Correct! A phrase that pushes you.
2.ko: Your inner voice plays too.

opts.a: "I can handle this at-bat"

3.q: Only bad players get nervous
3.ko: False: even the pros feel nerves.

4.q: What should you think about with the routine?
4.ok: That's it! One play at a time.
4.ko: Everything else waits its turn.

opts.a: Only the next play

5.q: Put the routine in order: breathe slowly, look at a fixed point, short phrase, think about the next play
5.ko: Breathe, look, tell yourself and play.

6.q: A fixed point to look at can be the ball or your base
6.ko: True: a fixed point calms your head.

19.4.title: Letting go of the mistake and leading by example
19.4.objective: Let go of the mistake: no player gets it right every time; after failing, you breathe, learn one thing and keep going. And lead by example: arrive ready, cheer without making fun and lift up the teammate who failed.
demo: Every player fails: the best batter in the world fails many times.
The difference is in what happens afterward.
Letting go of a mistake works like this: you breathe, you ask yourself "what do I learn from this one?", just one thing, and on to the next play with your head up.
And look at the other side: when your teammate fails, the leader doesn't make fun of him or complain: he lifts him up. "The next one's yours."
Being a leader isn't bossing people by yelling: it's arriving ready, always cheering and being the first to help.
That's how a Hall of Famer behaves, on and off the field.

1.q: After a mistake, what does a good player do?
1.ok: That's it! Mistake let go, the game goes on.
1.ko: One lesson and on to what comes next.

opts.a: Breathes, learns one thing and moves on to the next play
opts.b: Keeps thinking about the mistake the whole game

2.q: Your teammate dropped a fly ball. What do you say to him?
2.ok: Correct! That's what a leader does.
2.ko: Lift up, never drag down.

opts.a: "The next one's yours" and you keep cheering
opts.c: Nothing, you ignore him the whole game

3.q: A leader is the one who bosses the others by yelling
3.ok: Good! A leader is an example.
3.ko: False: the one who cheers and helps leads, not the one who yells.

4.q: Even the best players in the world fail many times
4.ok: Correct! Failing is part of the game.
4.ko: True: nobody gets it right every time in baseball.

5.q: Which question helps you let go of a mistake?
5.ko: Learning turns the mistake into a teacher.

opts.a: "What do I learn from this play?"

6.q: When does a player show leadership?
6.ko: You don't need a title to lift up the team.

19.5.title: Practicing at home and the limits that protect
19.5.objective: Practice at home safely (open space, soft ball, no throwing against walls or glass, with an adult nearby) and respect the limits that protect: your league's rules about throwing and resting exist to look after arms that are still growing, and you follow them by asking the coach.
demo: Practicing at home helps a lot, if you do it with your head.

Find an open space, with no glass or things that can break; use a soft ball if you practice catches near the house; practice your swing where nobody is behind you; and make sure an adult knows you're practicing.
No throwing hard against a wall right next to a window.
And one last Hall of Fame idea: the safety limits that protect you.
Your league sets rules to look after how many pitches a pitcher throws and how much he rests, because your arm is still growing.
Those limits aren't a punishment: they're a shield.
Your coach knows which ones apply to you: ask him and always respect them, even if you feel strong.

1.ok: That's it! Practice with your head.
1.ko: Safe at home is serious baseball too.

2.q: What are your league's limits on pitches and rest for?
2.ko: Limits that protect, not that punish.

3.ko: Each league and age has its own.

opts.a: Your coach

4.ok: Good! You always respect them.
4.ko: False: feeling strong doesn't erase the shield.

5.q: Practicing your swing where nobody is behind you is part of safety
5.ko: True: nobody goes behind the swing.

6.q: Your arm feels tired during practice at home. What do you do (review)?
6.ok: Good! Pain or strange tiredness means stop (review).
6.ko: Your arm matters more than practice.

20.1.title: Rookie review: the field and your turn
20.1.objective: Final review of levels 1 to 4, marked as review: the diamond and its bases, the positions with their numbers, strike, ball, foul, strikeout and walk, all mixed up like in a real game.
demo: Big final review, part one: go back to your first day.
The diamond, your four bases in order, the positions and their scorer's numbers.

20.2.title: Prospect review: hitting, outs and bases
20.2.objective: Final review of levels 5 to 8, marked as review: hit, ground-rule double, force out and tag out, double play, tag up and the R/H/E scoreboard.
demo: Big final review, part two: the Prospect stage.
You got your first hit and learned that single, double and triple count bases; that if the ball bounces over the fence it's a ground-rule double;
that the force out is made by stepping on the base and the tag out by tagging the runner; that two outs in one play is a double play;

1.q: First base is open and the most dangerous batter is up. The defense sends him to first on purpose. What play is it?

opts.a: However my league defines it: ask your coach
opts.b: With the same number in every league

3.q: Runner on first: he takes off with the pitch and the batter looks for contact. What play is it?

5.q: Runner on third: the batter bunts and the runner scores. What play is it?

opts.a: With the pitch, before seeing the bunt
